stem_md: Let  $P$  be a given (non-degenerate) polyhedron. Prove that there is a constant  $c(P)>0$  with the following property: If a collection of  $n$  balls whose volumes sum to  $V$  contains the entire surface of  $P,$  then  $n>c(P)/V^2.$
solution_md:
Not a complete proof but a crude sketch of a start:

Any ball of radius  $r$  volume  $c_1r^3$  and the largest surface area of a part of a plane contained in the ball is  $c_2r^2.$  (We know what  $c_1$  and  $c_2$  are but those numbers are not important.) The polyhedron has a finite number of plane polygons. Consider covering the union of these polygons with  $n$  balls of radii  $r_i.$  Then if  $A$  is the area of the union of polygons, to cover it, we must have  $A\le c_2\sum_{i=1}^nr_i^2.$  The total volume of the balls is assumed to be  $V=c_1\sum_{i=1}^nr_i^3$ We now use a  $p$ -norm inequality. If  $0<p<q<\infty,$  we have  $\left(\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nx_i^p\right)^{\frac1p}\le \left(\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nx_i^q\right)^{\frac1q}$  (for positive  $x_i$ ). We are given that  $\sum_{i=1}^nr_i^3=\frac{V}{c_1}$  and  $\sum_{i=1}^nr_i^2\ge\frac{A}{c_2}.$  Thus:
\[\left(\frac{V}{nc_1}\right)^{\frac13}=\left(\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nr_i^3\right)^{\frac13}\ge\left(\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nr_i^2\right)^{\frac12}\ge\left(\frac{A}{nc_2}\right)^{\frac13}\]
Taking sixth powers of the outer ends of the above chain gets us that  $\frac{V^2}{n^2c_1^2}\ge\frac{A^3}{n^3c_2^3}.$  The rearranges to  $n\ge\frac{C}{V^2},$  where  $C$  is some combination of  $A, c_1,$  and  $c_2.$ For a complete proof, you would need do show that balls that intersect edges or vertices do not have enough of an effect to change the main lines of this argument.

Nearby faces can be arranged in arbitrarily complex ways, creating huge difficulties even in representing the polyhedron, and there is no easy way to simplify the distribution of faces with respect to our distribution of balls. The trick is to observe that you are only looking for a lower bound for n, and then note that any set of balls that covers the entire surface of P must necessarily cover the largest face of P (call that A).  That is, a lower bound n for covering A is automatically a lower bound n for covering all of P (presumably not a very tight  lower bound, but that doesn't matter).
Then, look at covering the (flat) face A by the circular cross section of the balls.  And again, a very rough lower bound is when the sum of the circular areas equals the area of A -- obviously not a tight bound, however!

stem_md: A round-robin tournament among  $2n$  teams lasted for  $2n-1$  days, as follows. On each day, every team played one game against another team, with one team winning and one team losing in each of the  $n$  games. Over the course of the tournament, each team played every other team exactly once. Can one necessarily choose one winning team from each day without choosing any team more than once?
solution_md: Consider the bipartite graph formed by the  $2n-1$  days and the  $2n$  teams, and connect edges if a team won on that day. This has degree  $n,$  so Hall's condition is obvious when  $k \le n.$  If  $k>n,$  let  $S$  be a set of  $k$  days. Suppose FTSOC there are less than  $k$  teams winning at least one day in  $S,$  or that there at least  $2n-k+1$  teams that lost every day in  $S.$  Then each of these teams must've played each of the other  $2n-k$  teams in the other  $2n-k-1$  days not in  $S,$  which is clearly impossible, contradiction. Thus, Hall's Condition is satisfied, so there exists a perfect matching from days to teams, which is what we want.  $\blacksquare$

Consider a bipartite graph  $G=(L \cup R, L \times R)$ , where the set  $L$  describes the set of teams ( $|L|=2n$ ), and the set  $R$  denote the set of days ( $|R|=2n-1$ ). Let an edge  $(t,d) \in G$  if for  $t \in L$  and  $d \in R$ , team  $t$  won on day  $d$ . The problem is then equivalent to asking whether the graph necessarily contains a matching of size  $2n-1$ , that is, if for every day we can find a unique team that won on that day to match it to.

By Hall's Theorem, that is true iff  $\forall S \subseteq R, |N(S)|\geq|S|$ , where  $N(S)=\{t\in L: \exists d\in S, (t,d)\in G\}$ . I claim this holds for any valid graph  $G$  based on the problem specifications.

Assume  $|N(S)|<|S|$ , and let  $t\in L\setminus N(S)$  be a team that did not win in any day in  $S$ . Since  $|N(S)|<|S|<2n=|L|$  such a team exists. But, on each of the days in  $S$ ,  $t$  must have played and lost to a different opponent, which means at least  $|S|$  teams must have won some game, so  $|N(S)|\geq|S|$ , which is a contradiction. Thus,  $|N(S)|\geq|S|$  for all  $S\subseteq R$  and so it is always possible to choose one winning team from each day without choosing any team more than once.

It is possible to select one winning team from each day without ever selecting the same more than once. To see this we will use proof by contradiction:

Suppose that you could not choose one winning team from each day without selecting one team at least two times. Let "A" and "B" be two distinct days that games were held on, and let "A" and "B" arbitraryily be the days we must choose some team, which we will call team #1, twice. Also suppose that we were able to select different teams for every other day in which games were played except on days "A" and "B". Since there are 2n teams, suppose we re-evaluate our decision to select team #1 for day "B" but not for day "A". Then on day "B" we have at least n-1 winning teams to choose from that are not team #1; it follows that out assumption that there is a winning team that we must select at least twice on two separate days was wrong since there are n-1 other winning days we could have chose from that weren't team #1. Hence it is possible to select one winning team from each day without ever selecting the same winning team twice.

Before completing the proof we would like to point out that we have assumed there are at least 4 teams in the above contradiction. To see that the case when there are 2 teams is true note that there is only one game on one day in this case, so we must be able to select one winner since there was only one winner to begin with.

q.e.d.

Let  $I_{2n-1}$  be the set  ${1,2,\ldots,2n-1}$  representing the turns of the tournament. Let  $T$  the set of teams. Our objective is to prove the existence of a injective function  $f: I_{2n-1} \rightarrow T$  such that for every  $i$  the team  $f(i)$  won in the  $i$ -th turn.

We will prove that for every set  $D \subset I_{2n-1}$  there are at least  $|D|$  teams that won at least one match in one of these turns, then by Hall's theorem the existence of the the function  $f$  is guaranted and this solves the problem.

Denote  $|D|$  by  $d$ . Denote by  $g$  the number of teams that won at least some match in one of the days of  $D$ . Label these winners by  $1, 2, \ldots, g$  and denote by  $x_i$  the number of wins of the team  $i$  in the turns of  $D$ .

In every turn  $n$  wins occurs then the total number of wins is  $nd$  and thus \[x_1+x_2+\ldots+x_g=nd\]

Every team won at maximum  $d$  times. This gives \[x_1+x_2+\ldots+x_g \leq gd\]

Yet, in the turns of  $D$  some of the winners will play against each other. There are, beside the winners,  $2n-g$  teams, then every one of the winners played at least  $d-(2n-g)$  games against other winners in the turns of  $D$ . Thus there are at least  $\frac{1}{2}g(d-2n+g)$  games between in the winners in the turns of  $D$ . Thus we can improve the above bound \[x_1+x_2+\ldots+x_g \leq gd - \frac{1}{2}g(d-2n+g)\]
Then \[nd \leq gd - \frac{1}{2}g(d-2n+g)\] or, equivalentely \[(g-d)(g-2n) \leq 0\] how  $g\leq 2n$  then  $g \geq d$  and the solution is concluded.

Thus, those vertices must have edges only to the  $\ell$  vertices, and this is a contradiction, since every vertex has degree  $k$ , but  $\ell<k$ . Thus, Hall's condition holds, so we're done.

The answer is yes by Hall's theorem. In particular, consider the bipartite graph between  $D$ , the days in the tournament, and  $T$ , the teams in the tournament, where  $d \in D$  and  $t \in T$  are connected if team  $t$  won a game on day  $d$ . We will show that this graph satisfies Hall's condition.

In particular, consider any  $k$  days of the tournament; for each day, exactly  $n$  teams won a game on that day. Thus, if  $k \leq n$ , then Hall's condition follows immediately.

If  $k \geq n+1$ , then suppose that Hall's condition is not true for some  $k$  days. It follows that at most  $k-1$  teams won a game during those  $k$  days, i.e.  $2n-k+1$  teams did not win a single game during those  $k$  days. Call these teams the ``losers". However, any losing team must have played another losing team within those  $k$  days (as there are only  $k-1$  winning teams), meaning that one of those two teams won a game during those  $k$  days. This is a contradiction.

So Hall's condition is satisfied and we have a perfect matching, as the problem requests.

It suffices to find a perfect matching between days of the competition and winning teams. To this end, we'll verify Hall's condition then apply Hall's marriage theorem.

Consider some set of  $k$  days. Each day produces  $n$  distinct winners, so assume  $k > n$ . Let  $\ell$  be the number of teams that do not win a single match in any of these  $k$  days. Now, since each team plays exactly  $k$  matches across these  $k$  days, we have

so there are at least  $k$  distinct winners across this set, and we're done.  $\square$

Moreover we shall see that  $\left(a_n-\log n \right)_{n\ge 1}\to 0$ .
 As  $\Delta a_n=e^{-a_n}$ , computing the limit of  $\left(a_n-\log n\right)_{n\ge 1}$  is same as computing the limit of  $\left(\log(\Delta a_n \times n)\right)_{n\ge 1}$ . Our primary goal is to find an appropriate upper bound for  $\Delta a_n$  and we shall see that this can be achieved by evaluating the Riemann lower sum of the function  $e^x$  in the interval  $[1, a_n]$  (idea borrowed from @Xanthos C. We will show that in fact,  $\lim_{n\to\infty}(a_n-\log n)=0.$ A lemma we will use (from Taylor's theorem): there is a positive constant  $C$  such that if  $0\le x\le 1,$  then  $1+x\le e^x\le 1+x+Cx^2.$ Let  $b_n=e^{a_n}$  so that  $a_n = \log(b_n).$  The recursion becomes  $\log(b_{n+1})=\log(b_n)+\frac1{b_n}.$  Exponentiate that to get
\[b_{n+1}=b_n\cdot e^{1/b_n}.\]
Note that  $b_n$  is increasing and clearly  $b_n\ge 1$  so that  $\frac1{b_n}\le 1.$ By the estimate we gave above:
\begin{align*}b_n\left(1+\frac1{b_n}\right)&\le b_{n+1}\le b_n\left(1+\frac1{b_n}+\frac{C}{b_n^2}\right)
b_n+1&\le b_{n+1}\le b_n+1+\frac{C}{b_n}
1&\le b_{n+1}-b_n\le 1+\frac{C}{b_n}\end{align*}
The left hand inequality, plus an induction, assures us that  $b_n\ge n.$  Then we can write the right hand inequality as  $b_{n+1}-b_n\le 1+\frac{C}n.$  Sum this and we get a partial sum of the harmonic series. The known growth rate of the harmonic series tells us that  $n\le b_n\le n+\alpha+C\log n$  for some constant  $\alpha.$  Take the logarithm of this to get
\[\log n\le \log(b_n)\le \log(n+\alpha+ C\log n)=\log n+\log\left(1+\frac{\alpha}n+\frac{C\log n}n\right)\]
\[0\le a_n-\log n\le \log\left(1+\frac{\alpha}n+\frac{C\log n}n\right)\]
Since the right hand side of this tends to zero as  $n\to\infty,$  we get that the quantity  $(a_n-\log n)$  is squeezed to zero.

From  $a_{n+1} = a_{n} + e^{-a_n}$ , we get that  $a_n$  is strictly increasing, and that  $e^{a_n}(a_{n+1}-a_n) = 1$ . 

Since  $e^x$  is strictly increasing, a left endpoint Riemann sum will underestimate the value of an integral, i.e.:  $e^{a_n}-e $   $= \int_{1}^{a_n}e^x\,dx $   $> \sum_{k = 0}^{n-1}e^{a_k}(a_{k+1}-a_k) $   $= \sum_{k = 0}^{n-1} 1 = n$ Thus,  $a_n > \log(n+e)$ , and  $a_n - \log n > \log(1+\tfrac{e}{n}) \to 0$  as  $n \to \infty$ . 

Since  $e^x$  is strictly increasing, a right endpoint Riemann sum will overestimate the value of an integral, i.e.:  $e^{a_n}-e $   $= \int_{1}^{a_n}e^x\,dx $   $< \sum_{k = 0}^{n-1}e^{a_{k+1}}(a_{k+1}-a_k) $   $= \sum_{k = 0}^{n-1} e^{e^{-a_k}}\cdot e^{a_k}(a_{k+1}-a_k) $   $< \sum_{k = 0}^{n-1} e^{\tfrac{1}{k+e}} = : S_n$  

Thus,  $a_n < \log(S_n+e)$ , and  $a_n - \log n < \log(\tfrac{1}{n}S_n+\tfrac{e}{n})$ . 

Since  $\lim_{k \to \infty}e^{\tfrac{1}{k+e}} = 1$ , we have  $\lim_{n \to \infty}\dfrac{1}{n}S_n = 1$ . Thus,  $\log(\tfrac{1}{n}S_n+\tfrac{e}{n}) \to \log(1+0) = 0$  as  $n \to \infty$ . 

From this, we can conclude that  $\lim_{n \to \infty}(a_n - \log n) = 0$ .

We claim the answer is yes. For  $n \geq 1$ , let  $b_n = a_n - \ln n$ . We wish to show that  $\{b_n\}$  converges. Note that we have  $b_1 = a_1 > 0$ .  Substituting  $a_n = b_n + \ln n$  into our recurrence  $a_{n+1} = a_n + e^{-a_n}$  gives  $b_{n+1} = b_n + \ln(\frac{n}{n+1}) + \frac{e^{-b_n}}{n}$ . 

We claim that  $b_n \geq 0$  for all  $n$ .  Note that since  $e^x \geq x+1$  for all real  $x$ , we have  $e^{-b_n} \geq 1 - b_n$ . Additionally, for  $x = \frac{1}{n}$  we have  $e^{\frac{1}{n}} \geq 1 + \frac{1}{n}$ , which rearranges to  $\frac{1}{n} + \ln(\frac{n}{n+1}) \geq 0$ . Thus, \[ b_{n+1} = b_n + \ln(\frac{n}{n+1}) + \frac{e^{-b_n}}{n} \geq b_n + \ln(\frac{n}{n+1}) + \frac{1-b_n}{n} \geq \frac{1}{n} + \ln(\frac{n}{n+1})+ b_n (1 - \frac{1}{n}) \geq b_n (1 - \frac{1}{n}). \]
Since  $b_1, b_2 > 0$ , it follows by induction that  $b_n > 0$  for all  $n$ . 

It follows that 
\[ b_{n+1} = b_n + \ln(\frac{n}{n+1}) + \frac{e^{-b_n}}{n} \leq b_n + \frac{1}{n} - \ln(1 + \frac{1}{n+1}) = b_n + \frac{1}{2n^2} - O(\frac{1}{n^3}), \]
so there is some positive constant  $c$  for which  $b_{n+1} \leq b_n + \frac{c}{n^2}$  for all  $n$ . It follows that for all  $n>1$  and  $k>0$  that 
\[ b_{n+k} - b_n = \sum_{i=n}^{n+c-1} (b_{i+1} - b_i) \leq \sum_{i=n}^{n+c-1} \frac{c}{i^2} < \sum_{i=n}^{\infty} \frac{c}{i^2} < c \int_{i=n-1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{i^2} = \frac{c}{n-1}. \]

Since  $\{b_n\}$  is bounded from below, it has a limit inferior  $L$ . Let  $\epsilon$  be any positive real number. Then there is some  $N$  such that for all  $n>N$ , it holds that  $b_n > L - \epsilon$ . There also exist arbitrarily large  $M$  with  $b_M < L + \frac{\epsilon}{2}$ . Take any such  $M$  for which  $\frac{c}{M-1} < \frac{\epsilon}{2}$ . Then for all  $n > \max(M,N)$ , we have  $b_n > L - \epsilon$  and  $b_n < b_M + (b_n - b_M) < (L + \frac{\epsilon}{2}) + \frac{\epsilon}{2} = L + \epsilon$ , i.e.,  $|b_n - L| < \epsilon$ . Thus,  $\{b_i\}$  converges to  $L$ , as desired. 

*Note*: It's not too hard to show from here that we must have  $L=0$ . Since  $b_i \geq 0$ ,  $L \geq 0$ , so we suppose for the sake of contradiction that  $L>0$ . If we take  $\epsilon = \frac{L}{2}$ , then there is some  $N$  such that whenever  $n>N$  it holds that  $b_n > \epsilon$ . Now,
\begin{align*}
b_{n+1} 
&= b_n + \ln(\frac{n}{n+1}) + \frac{e^{-b_n}}{n} = b_n - \ln(1 + \frac{1}{n}) + \frac{e^{-b_n}}{n} 
&= b_n - \frac{1}{n} + O(\frac{1}{n^2}) + \frac{e^{-b_n}}{n} = b_n + \frac{e^{-b_n} - 1}{n} + O(\frac{1}{n^2}) 
&\leq b_n + O(\frac{1}{n^2}) + \frac{e^{-\epsilon} - 1}{n}
\end{align*}
Summing these from  $N$  to  $N+m$  for some  $m$ , we have
\[b_{N+m} \leq b_N + O(\frac{1}{N+m}) + (e^{-\epsilon} - 1) \sum_{i=N}^{N+m} \frac{1}{i}, \]
which is impossible since  $e^{-\epsilon} - 1 < 0$  and  $\sum_{i=N}^{N+m} \frac{1}{i}$  diverges as  $m$  goes to infinity.

If  $a_n$  was convergent, it would be null, which is absurd. Therefore,  $a_n$  is divergent.

Now, notice that  ${\displaystyle \lim_{n\to\infty}(e^{a_{n+1}}-e^{a_n}) = \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{e^{e^{-a_n}}-1}{e^{-a_n}}}$ .

The Cauchy criterion for $(x_n)_{n=1}^\infty$ converging is that $\lim_{N\to\infty}\sup_{m,n\geq N}|x_m-x_n|=0$ , not that $\lim_{n\to\infty}|x_{n+1}-x_n|=0$ . That the second condition is not sufficient can be seen easily with a simple counterexample (namely, $x_n=\sum_{j=1}^n\frac 1j$ ).

There's a fairly well-established tradition of misdirection in what Putnam questions claim to be asking for. One classic example from a couple of years back: an $n\times n$ determinant with entries given trigonometrically, and the question was about the limit of the determinant as $n\to\infty.$ So that makes it a calculus/analysis question, and there will be estimates and inequalities and growth rates and epsilons? stem_md: Let  $p$  be an odd prime number such that  $p\equiv 2\pmod{3}.$  Define a permutation  $\pi$  of the residue classes modulo  $p$  by  $\pi(x)\equiv x^3\pmod{p}.$  Show that  $\pi$  is an even permutation if and only if  $p\equiv 3\pmod{4}.$
solution_md:
Let  $\pi$  instead be the permutation on  $[p-1]$ , which is equivalent. We determine evenness of  $\pi$  by looking at the cycle count.

Let  $r$  be a primitive root mod  $p$ . The cycle length from  $x = r^k$  is the smallest positive integer  $\ell$  such that  $k 3^\ell \equiv k \pmod{p-1}$ . Setting  $g = (p-1) / \gcd(p-1, k)$ , we want  $g \mid 3^\ell$ . Note that there are  $\varphi(g)$  values of  $k$  for this value of  $g$ .

For any integer  $m$  let  $\operatorname{ord}_m(3)$  denote the smallest positive integer  $\ell$  such that  $m \mid 3^\ell-1$ . It's known that  $\operatorname{ord}_m(3) \mid \varphi(m)$  for any  $m$ .

The cycle count of  $\pi$  is now given by \[ S = \sum_{g \mid p-1} \frac{\varphi(g)}{\operatorname{ord}_g(3)}. \] As such,  $\pi$  is an even permutation if and only if  $S$  is even. Denote the summand by  $f(g)$ . We now analyze this sum. Let  $q_1$  and  $q_2$  be odd primes, and  $k_1$ ,  $k_2$ , and  $m$  be positive integers.  
- Consider  $f(q_1^{k_1} q_2^{k_2} m)$ , which is given by \[ f_1 = \frac{\varphi(q_1^{k_1}) \varphi(q_2^{k_2}) \varphi(m)} {\operatorname{lcm}(\operatorname{ord}_{Q_1}(3), \operatorname{ord}_{Q_2}(3), \operatorname{ord}_m(3))} \] where  $Q_i = q_i^{k_i}$ . If the  $\operatorname{lcm}$  in the denominator was instead a product, the expression would still be an integer  $f_2$  dividing  $f_1$ .

If  $f_2$  is even then so is  $f_1$ . Otherwise, since  $\varphi(Q_1)$  and  $\varphi(Q_2)$  are both even,  $\operatorname{ord}_{Q_1}(3)$  and  $\operatorname{ord}_{Q_2}(3)$  must also be even (they must in fact match the  $\nu_2$ ), and then the  $\operatorname{lcm}$  removes at least one factor of  $2$  from the denominator, making  $f_1$  even.
In either case,  $f(q_1^{k_1} q_2^{k_2} m)$  is even.
- The same analysis still works when  $q_1^{k_1}$  is replaced by  $4$ . These terms are also even.
- Since  $\operatorname{ord}_2(3) = 1$  and  $\varphi(2) = 1$ , we have  $f(2 q_1^{k_1}) = f(q_1^{k_1})$  always.
- Since  $3$  is not a primitive root mod  $2^k$  for  $k \geq 3$ , we have  $f(2^k)$  even (in fact it's always  $2$ ).
 Discarding the even terms and reducing mod  $2$ , we have \[ S \equiv \sum_{q^k \mid p-1} f(q^k) + \sum_{2q^k \mid p-1} f(2q^k) + [4 \mid p-1] \equiv [4 \mid p-1] \pmod 2, \] since the  $f(q^k)$  and  $f(2q^k)$  terms exactly cancel out.

Hence  $S$  is odd if and only if  $4 \mid p-1$ . This means  $\pi$  is even if and only if  $p \equiv 3 \pmod 4$ , which was what we wanted.  $\blacksquare$

A key point is that  $x^2\equiv -1\pmod{p}$  has solutions only if  $p\equiv 1\pmod{4}.$ We also note that for any  $p,$   $\pi(0)=0,\pi(1)=1,$  and  $\pi(-1)=-1.$  So the ``active" part of the permutation concerns what it does for the other  $p-3$  elements.

Suppose that  $p\equiv 3\pmod {4}.$  Chose  $a\notin\{0,1,-1\}$  and consider the sequence  $a,\pi(a),\pi^2(a),\dots$  which can also be written as  $a,a^3,a^9,a^{27},\dots.$  This repeats itself as a cycle, which becomes one cycle of the permutation. Can any of the elements on this list be  $-a?$  No, because  $a^{3^k}=-a$  would mean that  $a^{2j}\equiv -1$  for some  $j,$  which would make  $a^j$  a square root of  $-1,$  and that can't happen. Hence, the cycle that begins with  $a$  is disjoint from the cycle that begins with  $-a.$  But that latter cycle, namely  $-a, -a^3, -a^9,\dots,$  must have exactly the same cycle structure and cycle length as our original cycle.

This shows that our permutation can be completely partitioned into pairs of cycles of the same length. The product of two disjoint cycles of the same length is always even, and hence our overall permutation is even.

Next we suppose that  $p\equiv 1\pmod{4}.$  The equation  $x^2=-1$  has exactly two solutions. The multiplicative group (Z/p)^* is cyclic of order p-1.
If x in (Z/p)^* has order d, then so do all elements of x's cycle
{x, x^3, x^9, .. } (use: p is 2 mod 3).   The number of cycles
consisting of elements of order d is phi(d)/f(d) where

  phi(d) = the number of elements of order d
         = order of the group (Z/d)^* = Euler phi.

  f(d)   = length of the cycle = the order of 3 inside (Z/d)^*

We are asked to compute S mod 2 where  S := sum phi(d)/f(d)
and the sum is taken over all:   d|p-1 and 2|f(d)   (only cycles of
even length contribute to the sign of the permutation).

If d is odd, then phi(d)/f(d) = phi(2*d)/f(2*d),   so the sum over odd d's
cancels, mod 2, the sum over the 2*odd d's.  So to find S mod 2 it suffices
to sum over d's with 4|d.

If p is 3 mod 4, then there are no such d's,  so then S (and hence the
permutation) is even.

If p is 1 mod 4, then d=4 contributes phi(d)/f(d) = 2/2 = 1 to S.
Remains to count:  d=8, 12, 16, ...
For those d's,  (Z/d)^* is isomorphic to C2 x E for some group E of even order.
That implies that the maximal 2-power dividing f(d) is smaller than that
for phi(d). So phi(d)/f(d) is even and does not contribute to S mod 2.
So S (and hence the permutation) is odd when p is 1 mod 4.

This solution is similar to Zhero's. I will calculate the same product, but I do my calculation in  $\mathbb F_{p^2}$ .                                                   
                                                                                                                                                                        
Let  $\omega\in\mathbb F_{p^2}$  be a non-trivial third root of unity, which has minimal polynomial  $\omega^2+\omega+1$ . The conjugate of  $\omega$  is  $\omega^2=-1-\omega$ . Note that  $\{1,\omega\}$  is a basis for  $\mathbb F_{p^2}$  over  $\mathbb F_p$ . I'll use the fact that the product of all of the units in a finite field gives  $-1$  (since each element can be paired with its inverse, except for  $1$  and  $-1$ ; c.f. the proof of Wilson's theorem.) I also use the fact that  $(a+b)^p=a^p+b^p$  in characteristic  $p$  (you could also finish this solution off with quadratic reciprocity.)                                                                                            
                                                                                                                                                                        
\begin{align*}                                                                                                                                                          
\prod_{\{x,y\}\in{\mathbb F_p \choose 2}} \frac {x^3-y^3}{x-y}                                                                                                          
&= \prod_{\{x,y\}\in{\mathbb F_p \choose 2}} (x-\omega y)(x-\omega^2 y)                                                                                               
&= \left(-\omega^2\right)^{{p \choose 2}}\prod_{\{x,y\}\in{\mathbb F_p \choose 2}} (x-\omega y)(y-\omega x)                                                           
&= \left(-\omega^2\right)^{{p \choose 2}}\prod_{(x,y)\in \mathbb F_p \times \mathbb F_p\ :\ x\ne y} (x-\omega y)                                                      
&= \left(-\omega^2\right)^{{p \choose 2}} \left(\prod_{(x,y)\in\mathbb F_p\times\mathbb F_p\ :\ (x,y)\ne (0,0)} (x-\omega y)\right)\left(\prod_{x\in \mathbb F_p^{\times}} (x-\omega x)\right)^{-1}                                                                                                                                           
&= \left(-\omega^2\right)^{{p \choose 2}}\left(1-\omega\right)^{1-p}\left(\prod_{z\in\mathbb F_{p^2}^{\times}} z\right)\left(\prod_{x\in \mathbb F_p^{\times}} x\right)^{-1}                                                                                                                                                                  
&= \left(-\omega^2\right)^{{p \choose 2}}\left(1-\omega\right)^{1-p}                                                                                                  
&= \left(-1\right)^{\frac {p(p-1)} 2}\omega^{p(p-1)}\left(1-\omega\right)\left(\left(1-\omega\right)^{p}\right)^{-1}                                                  
&= \left(-1\right)^{\frac {p-1} 2}\omega^{2}\left(1-\omega\right)\left(1-\omega^p\right)^{-1}                                                                         
&= \left(-1\right)^{\frac {p-1} 2}\left(\omega^2-1\right)\left(1-\omega^2\right)^{-1}=(-1)^{\frac {p+1} 2}                                                              
\end{align*}

As mentioned in other solutions, we wish to determine the sign of multiplication by  $3$  on  $\mathbb{Z}/(p-1)$ . This is the same as the Frobenius element at  $3$  acting on the roots of  $f(x)=x^{p-1}-1$ , and to determine its sign we have to look at its action on the square root of the discriminant of this polynomial, which is equivalent to asking whether  $3$  splits in this extension. This discriminant is easily seen to be  $(-1)^{\binom{p-1}{2}}$  times the product  $\prod_{x^{p-1}=1} f'(x) =- (p-1)^{p-1}$ , which is a square. Therefore, if  $p \equiv 3 \pmod{4}$ , then  $\binom{p-1}{2}$  is odd, so adjoining the square root of the discriminant gives  $\mathbb{Q}$ , so  $3$  splits tautologically, and the permutation is even. If  $p \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$ , then the extension is  $\mathbb{Q}(i)$ , in which  $3$  does not split, so the permutation is odd.

Note that the sign of the permutation is given by \[S:=\prod_{0\le i<j\le p-1}\frac{j^3-i^3}{j-i}\pmod{p},\] as this counts the number of inversions. We see that \[S=\prod_{0\le i<j\le p-1}(i^2+ij+j^2).\] We have the following key lemma.**Lemma:**  Fix some  $a\in \mathbb{F}_p$ . The number of pairs  $(x,y)\in\mathbb{F}_p^2$  such that  $x^2+xy+y^2=a$  is  $p+1$ , assuming that  $p\equiv 2\pmod{3}$ .

*Proof:*  Note that  $\mathbb{F}_{p^2}=\mathbb{F}_p[\omega]$  where  $\omega^2+\omega+1=0$ , since  $X^2+X+1$  is an irreducible quadratic polynomial over  $\mathbb{F}_p[X]$  (this is because  $p\equiv 2\pmod{3}$ ). Let  $\sigma:\mathbb{F}_{p^2}\to\mathbb{F}_{p^2}$  given by  $\sigma(t)=t^p$  be the Frobenius endomporhism. We see that  $\sigma(a+b\omega)=a+b\omega^2=(a-b)-b\omega$ .

Now, the equation  $x^2+xy+y^2=a$  turns into \[(x+y\omega)(x+y\omega^2)=a.\] Note that the pairs  $(x,y)$  are in bijection with  $\mathbb{F}_{p^2}$  where  $(x,y)\mapsto x+y\omega$ , so it suffices to find the number of  $z\in\mathbb{F}_{p^2}$  such that \[z\cdot z^p=a.\] We claim that there are exactly  $p+1$  solutions in  $z$  to  $z^{p+1}=a$ . To see this, note that \[X^{p+1}-a\mid X^{(p+1)(p-1)}-a^{p-1}=X^{p^2-1}-1,\] so \[X^{p+1}-a\mid X^{p^2}-X=\prod_{k\in\mathbb{F}_{p^2}}(X-k),\] where we are working over  $\mathbb{F}_{p^2}[X]$ . Thus,  $X^{p+1}-a$  has exactly  $p+1$  distinct roots among  $\mathbb{F}_{p^2}$ , which proves the lemma.  $\blacksquare$ We see that  $i^2+i\cdot i+i^2=a$  has a solution for  $i$  if and only if  $\left(\frac{3a}{p}\right)=1$ , so the number of  $0\le i<j\le p-1$  such that  $i^2+ij+j^2=a$  is \[\frac{p-\left(\frac{3a}{p}\right)}{2}.\] Thus, \[S=\prod_{a\in\mathbb{F}_p^\times}a^{\frac{p-\left(\frac{3a}{p}\right)}{2}}.\] Letting  $g$  be a primitive root mod  $p$ , we see that  $S=g^s$  where \[s=\sum_{k=0}^{p-2}k\left[\frac{p-\left(\frac{3}{p}\right)(-1)^k}{2}\right]=\frac{p(p-1)(p-2)}{4}-\left(\frac{3}{p}\right)\frac{p-1}{4}.\] Since  $g^{\frac{p-1}{2}}=-1$ , we see that \[S=(-1)^{\frac{p(p-2)-\left(\frac{3}{p}\right)}{2}}.\] We see that  $S=+1$  if and only if \[p(p-2)-\left(\frac{3}{p}\right)\equiv 0\pmod{4},\] which is if and only if  $p\equiv 3\pmod{4}$ . This solves the problem.

We can consider the number of cycles in the permutation. The parity of the permutation is the same as (number of elements) - (number of cycles)

So we want to show the number of cycles is odd if and only if  $p\equiv 1(\bmod\; 4)$ Let  $ord_k(x)$  for any integer  $k$  (not just k prime) be defined as the smallest positive integer  $n$  such that  $x^n\equiv 1(\bmod\; k)$ , if it exists.

Claim 1: The number of components is   $$ \sum\limits_{k\mid p-1} \frac{\varphi(k)}{ord_k(3)} $$  Proof: Let  $S_k=\{x:ord_p(x)=k\}$ . By Mobius inversion,  $|S_k|=\varphi(k).$  

Since  $\gcd(3,p-1)=1,  ord_p(x^3)=ord_p(x)$ . Therefore,  $\pi$  creates cycles in one  $S_i$  only. A cycle will be reached if  $\pi^n(x)= x(\bmod\; p) \leftrightarrow p\mid x^{3^n-1}-1$ . The smallest such  $n$  is also the smallest  $n$  such that  $k\mid 3^n-1$ , which is  $ord_k(3)$ . Therefore, inside  $S_k$  there are  $\frac{|S_k|}{ord_k(3)}=\frac{\varphi(k)}{ord_k(3)}$  cycles. Summing over all  $k\mid p-1$  yields the desired result.


Let's find which  $k$  makes  $\frac{\varphi(k)}{ord_k(3)}$  odd

Proof: let  $k=\prod q_i^{e_i}$ Then  $\varphi(k)=\prod (q_i-1)q_i^{e_i-1}$  $ord_k(3)=lcm (ord_{q_i^{e_i}}(3)) | lcm (q_i-1)q_i^{e_i-1}$  $\nu_2(ord_k(3))\le \max (\nu_2((q_i-1))+(e_i-1)\nu_2(q_i))$ However, we want  $\nu_2(ord_k(3))=\nu_2(\varphi(k))=\sum (\nu_2((q_i-1))+(e_i-1)\nu_2(q_i))$ Therefore, exactly one of  $\nu_2((q_i-1))+(e_i-1)\nu_2(q_i)$ 's is nonzero. This is positive if  $q_i$  is odd or if  $q_i=2$  and  $e_i>1$ . Since even  $\frac{\varphi(k)}{ord_k(3)}$  doesn't affect the parity of the desired sum, we only concentrate on those  $k$ .

Also, for any odd number  $q$ ,  $\varphi(q)=\varphi(2q), ord_q(3)=ord_{2q}(3)$ , so  $q$  can be paired with  $2q$ . 

Thus this sum only needs to be done for  $4|k$  where  $k$  is a power of 2. Note  $\varphi(4)=ord_4(3)=2$  but  $\varphi(2^k)=2^{k-1}$  while  $ord_{2^k}(3)=2^{k-2}$ . Therefore,  $\sum\limits_{k\mid p-1} \frac{\varphi(k)}{ord_k(3)}$  is odd if and only if  $4\mid p-1$ , as desired.

The permutation is even if and only if the number  $n$  of cycles  $x\mapsto x^3\mapsto x^9\mapsto \cdots \mapsto x^{3^k} = x$  is odd, since the number of swaps needed to generate the permutation is  $p-n$ . Equivalently, we want to check if the number  $n-1$  of cycles  $x\mapsto x^3\mapsto x^9\mapsto \cdots \mapsto x^{3^k}=x$  with  $x\ne 0$  is even. Let  $g$  denote a primitive root modulo  $p$  so a cycle is equivalent to choosing  $m\pmod{p-1}$  so that  $m\mapsto 3m\mapsto 9m\mapsto \cdots \mapsto 3^km = m$  is a cycle mod  $p-1$ . For a particular integer  $s\ge 1$  with  $\gcd(3,s)=1$ , let  $o_s(3)$  denote the order of  $3$  modulo  $s$ . Then it follows that the number of cycles counted by  $n-1$  is
\[\sum_{d\mid p-1} \frac{\phi(d)}{o_d(3)}.\]
Remark that  $\phi(d)/o_d(3)$  is odd if and only if  $3^{\phi(d)/2}$  is not  $1$  modulo  $d$ . Observe that if  $d$  can be written as  $p^kd'$  with with  $p$  an odd prime,  $p\nmid d'$  and  $2\mid \phi(d')$ , then  $p^{k-1}(p-1)\mid p^{k-1}(p-1)\phi(d')/2=\phi(d)/2$  and  $\phi(d')\mid p^{k-1}(p-1)\phi(d')/2$ . As  $2\mid \phi(d')$  unless  $d'$  is  $2$  or  $1$ , this means that the only possible  $d$  we care about are powers of two, a prime power  $p^k$ , and twice a prime power. Remark that for a prime power  $p^k$ ,  $\phi(p^k)=\phi(2p^k)$  and since  $2\mid 3^t-1$  for any nonnegative integer  $t$ ,  $p^k\mid 3^t-1$  if and only if  $2p^k\mid 3^t-1$ . Thus terms  $\phi(p^k)/o_{p^k}(s)$  and  $\phi(2p^k)/o_{2p^k}(s)$  can be paired, meaning we are left with
\[\sum_{2^k\mid p-1}\frac{\phi(2^k)}{o_{2^k}(3)}.\]
Since the Carmichael number of  $2^k$  for  $k\ge 3$  is  $2^{k-2}$ , we only care about  $k\le 2$ . Then  $\phi(1)/o_1(3)=1,\phi(2)/o_2(3)=1,\phi(4)/o_4(3)=1$ . We have no choice about summing the first two because  $2\mid p-1$ , so this means that  $4\mid p-1$  if and only if  $n-1$  is odd if and only if the permutation is odd. Thus the problem statement follows.

Lot of interesting ideas in this thread. Here's one more solution:

For finite sets  $A,B$  and permutations  $\pi_1\in\mathbb S(A)$ ,  $\pi_2\in\mathbb S(B)$  we can define permutation  $\pi_1\times\pi_2\in\mathbb S(A\times B)$  in an obvious way. Then
\[\sigma(\pi_1\times\pi_2)=\sigma(\pi_1\times\mathrm{id}_B)\cdot\sigma(\mathrm{id}_A\times\pi_2)=\sigma(\pi_1)^{|B|}\sigma(\pi_2)^{|A|}.\]
As discussed above, the problem is equivalent to determining the sign of permutation given by multiplication by  $3$  on  $\mathbb Z/(p-1)$ . Let  $p-1=2^ab$  with  $2\nmid b$ . Then  $\mathbb Z/(p-1)\cong\mathbb Z/2^a\times\mathbb Z/b$  and the permutation given by multiplication by  $3$  on  $\mathbb Z/(p-1)$  is the product of permutations given by multiplication by  $3$  on  $\mathbb Z/2^a$  and  $\mathbb Z/b$ . Since  $2\mid|\mathbb Z/2^a|$  and  $2\nmid|\mathbb Z/b|$ , it follows from the above formula that the sign of multiplication by  $3$  on  $\mathbb Z/(p-1)$  is the same as the sign of multiplication by  $3$  on  $\mathbb Z/2^a$ .
First we determine the sign of permutation  $\pi_n$  given by multiplication  by  $3$  on  $\left(\mathbb Z/2^n\right)^\times$  for  $n\in\mathbb N_0$ . For  $n=0$  and  $n=1$  the permutation is even and for  $n=2$  it's odd. For  $k\in\mathbb N_0$  we have
\[v_2(3^{2^k}-1)=\begin{cases}1&k=0,k+2&k>0.\end{cases}\]
The first case is obvious, the second follows from the formula
\[3^{2^k}-1=(3^2-1)\prod_{i=1}^{k-1}\left(3^{2^i}+1\right)\]
where each factor in the product is divisible by  $2$  once (this is a special case of the LTE lemma). It follows that for  $n\ge3$  the order of  $3$  in  $\left(\mathbb Z/2^n\right)^\times$  is  $2^{n-2}$  and  $\pi_n$  composes of  $\big|\left(\mathbb Z/2^n\right)^\times\big|/2^{n-2}=2^{n-1}/2^{n-2}=2$  cycles of lenght  $2^{n-2}$ , and thus is even.
Finally, we have a decomposition
\[\mathbb Z/2^a=\bigsqcup_{n=0}^a2^{a-n}\left(\mathbb Z/2^n\right)^\times,\]
where we identify the class  $2^{a-n}[x]_{2^n}$  with  $[2^{a-n}x]_{2^a}$ , and thus the sign of multiplication by  $3$  on  $\mathbb Z/2^a$  is  $\prod_{n=0}^a\sigma(\pi_n)$ . It then follows from the above calculations that the permutation is even for  $a=1$  and odd for  $a\ge2$ , hence the result.

Let $p$ be an odd prime number such that $p\equiv 2\pmod{3}.$ Define a permutation $\pi$ of the residue classes modulo $p$ by $\pi(x)\equiv x^3\pmod{p}.$ Show that $\pi$ is an even permutation if and only if $p\equiv 3\pmod{4}.$
What a nice problem! More details would be needed, but the key idea is as follow: Note that \begin{align*} \pi \ \text{is odd} &\iff \ \text{there are odd number of even cycles} &\iff \ \text{there are odd number of cycles that contain } (a, -a) &\iff \ \text{there are odd number of cycles that contain } (a, -a, 1/a, -1/a) &\iff a^2 + 1 = 0 \pmod{p} &\iff p \equiv 1 \pmod{4} \end{align*} The first equivalence hold by definition. The second and third equivalence hold by pairing argument. The fourth equivalence, which I think is the most interesting (and hardest) insight of the problem, is to note that for any such cycle that contain $(a, -a, 1/a, -1/a)$ , then the both $-a$ and $1/a$ must be on the halfway point on the entire cycle, which means that they have to be the same element: $a = -\frac{1}{a} \iff a^2 + 1 = 0$ , and the rest follows.

solution_md:
Determine all integer solutions $(x, y)$ of the equation \[(x - 1)x(x + 1) + (y - 1)y(y + 1) = 24 - 9xy\mbox{.}\]
$\iff$ $(x+y-3)(x^2-xy+y^2+3x+3y+8)=0$ So a first family of solutions $(x,y)=(n,3-n)$ And it remains to solve $x^2-xy+y^2+3x+3y+8=0$ $\iff$ $(2x-y+3)^2+3(y+3)^2=4$ and so : $2x-y+3=1$ and $y+3=1$ which gives $(x,y)=(-2,-2)$ $2x-y+3=1$ and $y+3=-1$ which gives $(x,y)=(-3,-4)$ $2x-y+3=-1$ and $y+3=1$ which gives $(x,y)=(-3,-2)$ $2x-y+3=-1$ and $y+3=-1$ which gives $(x,y)=(-4,-4)$ $2x-y+3=2$ and $y+3=0$ which gives $(x,y)=(-2,-3)$ $2x-y+3=-2$ and $y+3=0$ which gives $(x,y)=(-4,-3)$ Hence the answer : $\boxed{(x,y)\in\{(-2,-2),(-3,-4),(-3,-2),(-4;-4),(-2,-3),(-4,-3)\}\cup\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb Z}\{(n,3-n)\}}$

From [here](https://ssmr.ro/files/onm2012/solutii_7.pdf)
official solution**Problem 4.** We define the **reduced** form of a natural number \( A \) with \( n \) digits (\( n \geq 2 \)) as a number with \( n-1 \) digits obtained by deleting one of the digits of \( A \). For example, the reduced forms of 1024 are 124, 104, and 120. Determine how many seven-digit numbers cannot be written as the sum of a natural number \( A \) and a reduced form of \( A \). **Solution.** Let us call a number **convenient** if it can be written as the sum of a number and its reduced form, and **inconvenient** if it cannot be written in this way. The number \( A = a_1a_2a_3a_4a_5a_6a_7 \) and its reduced form \( B = a_1a_2a_3a_4a_5a_6 \) have the sum \( 11B + a_7 \), i.e., a number of at least 7 digits, greater than \( 11 \cdot 10^5 \), which does not give a remainder of 10 when divided by 11. By appropriately choosing the number \( B \) and the digit \( a_7 \), it follows that any number of 7 digits, greater than \( 11 \cdot 10^5 \), that does not give a remainder of 10 when divided by 11, is convenient. As a result, by appropriately choosing the number \( D \) and the digit \( c_6 \), it follows that any number of 7 digits, smaller than \( 11 \cdot 10^5 \), that does not give a remainder of 10 when divided by 11, is convenient. Thus, the inconvenient numbers are found in the set of 7-digit numbers that give a remainder of 10 when divided by 11. Since the sum of any natural number with any of its reduced forms, except the one obtained by removing the last digit, is an even number, it follows that 7-digit numbers of the form \( 22p + 21 \), where \( p \in \mathbb{N} \), are inconvenient. It remains to study the situation of 7-digit numbers of the form \( 22p + 10 \), where \( p \in \mathbb{N} \). We will show that these numbers can be written in the form \[ a_1a_2 \dots a_{n-2}a_{n-1}a_n + a_1a_2 \dots a_{n-2}a_n = 110 \cdot a_1a_2 \dots a_{n-2} + 10 \cdot a_{n-1} + 2a_n, \] where \( n \in \{6, 7\} \). Numbers of the form \( 22p + 10 \), \( p \in \mathbb{N} \), depending on the remainder of the division of \( p \) by 5, have one of the forms \( 110k + 10 \), \( 110k + 32 \), \( 110k + 54 \), \( 110k + 76 \), \( 110k + 98 \), where \( k \in \mathbb{N} \). By choosing \( k = \frac{a_1a_2 \dots a_{n-2}}{10} \) and, for example, \( (a_{n-1}, a_n) \in \{(1, 0), (3, 1), (5, 2), (7, 3), (9, 4)\} \), it follows that the numbers of the form \( 22p + 10 \), \( p \in \mathbb{N} \), are convenient. As a result, the inconvenient 7-digit numbers are those of the form \( 22p + 21 \), where \( p \in \mathbb{N} \). From \( 10^6 \leq 22p + 21 \leq 10^7 - 1 \), it follows that \( 45,454 \leq p \leq 454,545 \). Since \( p \) has 454,545 - 45,454 + 1 = 409,091 values, it follows that there are 409,091 inconvenient 7-digit numbers.

stem_md:
We consider the non-zero natural numbers  $(m, n)$  such that the numbers   $$ \frac{m^2 + 2n}{n^2 - 2m} \,\,\,\, and \,\,\, \frac{n^2 + 2m}{m^2-2n} $$   are integers.
a) Show that  $|m - n| \le 2$ :
b) Find all the pairs  $(m, n)$  with the property from hypothesis  $a$ .
solution_md:
We consider the non-zero natural numbers $(m, n)$ such that the numbers $$ \frac{m^2 + 2n}{n^2 - 2m} \,\,\,\, and \,\,\, \frac{n^2 + 2m}{m^2-2n} $$ are integers. a) Show that $|m - n| \le 2$ : b) Find all the pairs $(m, n)$ with the property from hypothesis $a$ .
From [here](https://ssmr.ro/files/onm2012/solutii_7.pdf)
the official solution. **Solution** **a)** Since \((m^2 - 2n)\) divides \((n^2 + 2m)\) and \(n^2 + 2m > 0\), it follows that \(m^2 - 2n \leq n^2 + 2m\), i.e., \((m - 1)^2 \leq (n + 1)^2\), so \(m \leq n + 2\). Similarly, \(n \leq m + 2\). Consequently, \(|m - n| \leq 2\) **b)** We assume \(n \geq m\). Then \(n \in \{m, m+1, m+2\}\). - If \(n = m\), then \(\frac{n^2 + 2n}{n^2 - 2m} = 1 + \frac{4}{n-2} \in \mathbb{Z}\), from which \(n \in \{1, 3, 4, 6\}\). We obtain the pairs \((n, m) \in \{(1,1), (3,3), (4,4), (6,6)\}\) - If \(n = m + 1\), then \(\frac{n^2 + 2n}{m^2 - 2m} = 1 + \frac{2m + 1}{m^2 + m + 1}\). For \(m \geq 3\), we have \(0 < \frac{8m}{m^2 + m + 1} < 1\), so \(\frac{n^2 + 2n}{m^2 - 2m} \notin \mathbb{Z}\). - For \(m = 1\), \(\frac{2m + 1}{m^2 + 1} = \frac{3}{2} \notin \mathbb{Z}\), and for \(m = 2\) \((n = 3)\) we have \(\frac{n^2 + 2n}{m^2 - 2m} = \frac{13}{2} \notin \mathbb{Z}\). Thus, in this case \(n + 1\) does not give us any solutions. - If \(n = m + 2\), then \(\frac{n^2 + 2n}{m^2 - 2m} = 1 + \frac{8m + 8}{m^2 - 2m - 4} \in \mathbb{Z}\). If \(n \geq 12\), then \(m^2 - 2m - 4 > 8m + 8\). Indeed, \(m^2 - 10m - 12 = m(m - 10) - 12 \geq 12 > 12 - 12 > 0\). It follows that for \(m \geq 12\) we have \(\frac{n^2 + 2n}{m^2 - 2m} \notin \mathbb{Z}\). For \(m \in \{1, 2, \ldots, 11\}\), we verify the pairs obtained and find that \(\frac{n^2 + 2n}{m^2 - 2m} \notin \mathbb{Z}\) for \((n, m) \in \{(2,4), (3,5), (4,6)\}\). **In conclusion, considering the symmetry of the fractions,** \((n, m) \in \{(1,1), (3,3), (4,4), (6,6),(2,4), (3,5), (4,6),(4,2), (5,3), (6,4)\}\).

stem_md: Determine the real numbers  $a, b, c, d$  so that  $$ ab + c + d = 3, \,\, bc + d + a = 5, \,\, cd + a + b = 2 \,\,\,\, and \,\,\,\,da + b + c = 6 $$
solution_md:
Subtracting we find  $(b-1)(c-a)=2,(c-1)(b-d)=3,(d-1)(a-c)=4,(a-1)(d-b)=3$ .
Taking  $a-1=A$  etc we find  $B(C-A)=2, C(B-D)=3,D(A-C)=4, A(D-B)=3$ .
We have  $B\not=D \implies A=-C$  and  $A\not=C\implies D=-2B$ .
Inserting that gives  $BC=1$ .
Rewriting  $ab+c+d=3$  gives  $AB+A+B+C+D=0\implies AB+B+D=0\iff (A-1)B=0\implies A=1,a=2,C=-1,c=0$ . From  $BC=1$  we have  $B=-1,D=2,b=0,d=3$ .
Hence  $(a,b,c,d)=(2,0,0,3)$ .

stem_md: The altitude $[BH]$ dropped onto the hypotenuse of a triangle $ABC$ intersects the bisectors $[AD]$ and $[CE]$ at $Q$ and $P$ respectively. Prove that the line passing through the midpoints of the segments $[QD]$ and $[PE]$ is parallel to the line $AC$ .
solution_md:
Well, see that triangles  $\triangle BEP, \triangle BQD$  are isosceles, hence if  $M, N$  are the midpoints of  $[PE]$ , respectively  $[QD]$ , we have  $BM\bot CE, BN\bot AD$ ,  $\angle MBP=\frac{\widehat C}{2}, \angle NBQ=\frac{\widehat A}{2}$ , i.e.  $BMIN$  is cyclic,  $I$  being the incenter. From  $\angle DBI=\angle MBN=45^\circ\implies \angle IBN = \angle MBP = \frac{\widehat C}{2}$ . From  $BMIN$  we get  $\angle NMI=\angle NBI=\angle MBP=\angle ACE = \frac{\widehat C}{2}$ , or  $MN\parallel AC$ .

stem_md: Find all functions $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ with the following property: for any open bounded interval $I$ , the set $f(I)$ is an open interval having the same length with $I$ .
solution_md:
We claim the answer is  $f(x)=\pm x + C$ . First, since the stipulations of the problem are symmetric with respect to translation, with loss of that particular generality (who needs that generality anyway?!)  $f(0)=0$ . **Lemma**: Considering neighborhoods of a point on the domain, we can get arbitrarily small bounds on the y-values for that interval as the neighborhoods grow smaller.**Proof:** This is basically a weaker restatement of the condition; I just put it as a lemma for clarity. This shows that we can treat  $(a,b)$  on the domain of  $f$  with the condition like  $[a,b]$  by considering neighborhoods of  $a$  and  $b$ .

Let the maximum and minimum values of  $f$  over  $(0,x),x>0$  be  $M$  and  $m$  respectively. By taking  $(-\epsilon,x),\epsilon \rightarrow 0$  from our lemma and the conditions we find that  $M-m=x$ . Suppose  $M>m$ . But then  $(-\epsilon,(M+x)/2),\epsilon \rightarrow 0$  also having  $M-m$  as its range shows that we must have  $M=x,m=0$ . Symmetrically,  $m>M$  shows that we need  $m=-x,M=0$ . Similar logic with flipped signs applies for  $x<0$ . Therefore,  $|f(x)|=x$  for all  $x$ . 

If we have  $f(a)=a$  and  $f(b)=-b$ , letting  $a<b$   $(a-\epsilon,b+\epsilon)$  and the condition shows  $a+b=b-a$  so that  $a=0$ , and symmetrically  $b<a$  means  $b=0$ . The result follows that  $f(x)=\pm x$ , and removing the  $f(0)=0$  restriction, we have our answer.

stem_md: Prove that if $n\ge 2$ is a natural number and $x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n$ are positive real numbers, then: \[4\left(\frac {x_1^3-x_2^3}{x_1+x_2}+\frac {x_2^3-x_3^3}{x_2+x_3}+\ldots+\frac {x_{n-1}^3-x_n^3}{x_{n-1}+x_n}+\frac {x_n^3-x_1^3}{x_n+x_1}\right)\le \le(x_1-x_2)^2+(x_2-x_3)^2+\ldots+(x_{n-1}-x_n)^2+(x_n-x_1)^2\, .\]
solution_md:
Prove that if $n\ge 2$ is a natural number and $x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n$ are positive real numbers, then: \[4\left(\frac {x_1^3-x_2^3}{x_1+x_2}+\frac {x_2^3-x_3^3}{x_2+x_3}+\ldots+\frac {x_{n-1}^3-x_n^3}{x_{n-1}+x_n}+\frac {x_n^3-x_1^3}{x_n+x_1}\right)\le \le(x_1-x_2)^2+(x_2-x_3)^2+\ldots+(x_{n-1}-x_n)^2+(x_n-x_1)^2\, .\]
Here is another proof: $4\sum \frac{x_1^3-x_2^3 }{x_1+x_2}=4\sum (x_1^2-x_1x_2+x_2^2)-8\sum \frac{x_2^3}{x_1+x_2}$ , so it remains to prove that: $8\sum x_1^2 \le 8\sum \frac{x_2^3}{x_1+x_2}+\sum (x_1+x_2)^2$ But this follows from am-gm: $8\sum \frac{x_2^3}{x_1+x_2}+\sum (x_1+x_2)^2=\sum \left( \frac{8x_2^3}{x_1+x_2}+ 2x_2(x_1+x_2) \right) \ge 8\sum x_2^2$ Equality holds when $x_1=...=x_n$ .

stem_md: On a table there are $k\ge 2$ piles having $n_1,n_2,\ldots,n_k$ pencils respectively. A *move* consists in choosing two piles having $a$ and $b$ pencils respectively, $a\ge b$ and transferring $b$ pencils from the first pile to the second one. Find the necessary and sufficient condition for $n_1,n_2,\ldots,n_k$ , such that there exists a succession of moves through which all pencils are transferred to the same pile.
solution_md:
Let  $k_i=\frac{n_i}{\gcd n}$ . We claim it is possible iff  $\sum k_i$  is a power of two.

We shall consider the reverse operation. Instead of  $(a,b)\mapsto (a-b,2b)$ , we take  $(x,y)\mapsto\left(\frac{x}{2},y+\frac{x}{2}\right)$ . Note that in this case,  $a=y+\frac{x}{2}>\frac{x}{2}=b$  is always true. The problem thus becomes what configurations of piles a single pile can map to using this reversal.

Let the single pile start with  $2^tN$  pencils, where  $N$  is odd. As pencils can only be shifted away from even piles, any move from that point on can only shift a multiple of  $N$  number of pencils, and the sum of all pencils is clearly constant, so necessity immediately follows. 

We'll look forwards again for sufficiency, but not before noting that by the above, the problem reduces to when the sum is  $2^t$ . We proceed by induction on  $t$ . First  $t=1$ , clearly, the result holds. Now, for arbitrary  $t$ , note that since  $\sum n_i=2^t$ , an even number of the  $n_i$  must be odd. We then sort them into arbitrary pairs and take  $(2p-1,2q-1)\mapsto(4p-2,2q-2p)$ . At this point, we have every  $n_i$  divisible by 2, so as before, the problem reduces to  $n_i/2$  summing to  $2^{t-1}$ , which has a solution by the inductive step..

The result follows.

stem_md: Let $M=\{x\in\mathbb{C}\, |\, |z|=1,\ \text{Re}\, z\in\mathbb{Q}\}\, .$ Prove that there exist infinitely many equilateral triangles in the complex plane having all affixes of their vertices in the set $M$ .
solution_md:
We want to find infinitely many angles  $\theta$  such that  $\cos \theta$ ,  $\cos (\theta + 120^\circ)$ , and  $\cos (\theta + 240^\circ)$  are all rational.  Since
\[\cos \theta + \cos (\theta + 120^\circ) + \cos (\theta + 240^\circ) = 0\]
for all  $\theta$ , it suffices to find infinitely many angles  $\theta$  such that both  $\cos \theta$  and  $\cos (\theta + 120^\circ)$  are rational.

Let  $t$  be any rational number, and let
\[x = \frac{3t^2 - 1}{3t^2 + 1}, \quad y = \frac{2t}{3t^2 + 1},\]
so  $x$  and  $y$  are also rational.  It is easy to check that  $x^2 + 3y^2 = 1$ .  Hence, there exists an angle such that  $\cos \theta = x$  and  $\sin \theta = y \sqrt{3}$ .  Then  $\cos \theta$  is rational, and
\begin{align*}
\cos (\theta + 120^\circ) &= \cos \theta \cos 120^\circ - \sin \theta \sin 120^\circ 
&= -\frac{1}{2} \cos \theta - \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \sin \theta 
&= -\frac{x + 3y}{2},
\end{align*}
which is also rational.

stem_md: Let $a$ , $b$ and $c$ be three complex numbers such that $a+b+c=0$ and $|a|=|b|=|c|=1$ . Prove that: \[3\le |z-a|+|z-b|+|z-c|\le 4,\] for any $z\in\mathbb{C}$ , $|z|\le 1\, .$
solution_md:
Let the numbers  $a,b,c$  form triangle  $ABC$  on the complex plane. If we consider the complex numbers  $a,b,c$  on the complex plane, the condition  $|a|=|b|=|c|=1$  tells us that the points lie on the unit circle, so triangle  $ABC$  has its circumcenter at the origin and has a circumradius equal to 1. Also, the condition  $a+b+c=0$  tells us that the centroid of triangle  $ABC$  is also the origin (the centroid and circumcenter coincide). This implies that triangle  $ABC$  is equilateral.

If we look at the geometric meaning of the inequality we must prove, it is simply that given any point inside or on the unit circle, the sum of the distances from the point to the vertices of triangle  $ABC$  is between 3 and 4. 

Now that we've turned this into a geometry problem, it's quite simple to see that the minimum sum of distances is 3 and occurs when  $z$  is at the origin. The maximum sum of distances is 4 and occurs when  $z$  is on the circle halfway between any two vertices.

stem_md: Let $n$ and $m$ be two natural numbers, $m\ge n\ge 2$ . Find the number of injective functions \[f\colon\{1,2,\ldots,n\}\to\{1,2,\ldots,m\}\] such that there exists a unique number $i\in\{1,2,\ldots,n-1\}$ for which $f(i)>f(i+1)\, .$
solution_md:
We claim the answer is  $\binom{m}{n}(2^n-n-1)$  (1). 

To prove it, first note that this is clearly just  $\binom{m}{n}$  times the number of such functions from  $S=\{1,2,\ldots,n\}$  to itself as only relative magnitudes matter, so we turn to that simpler problem. This is just the number of permutations s.t. there is only one  $f(i)>f(i+1)$ . Consider the sequences  $f(1),f(2),\ldots,f(i)$  and  $f(i+1),\ldots,f(n)$ . They are both by assumption increasing, and form a partition of  $S$ ; thus, for any such permutation, we can characterize it by the set  $A=\{f(1),f(2),\ldots,f(i)\}$  of the first  $i$  terms, as the order of that set and the elements and order of the next,  $S\setminus A = B$  are then determined. Similarly, letting any subset of  $S$  be  $A$  will give a distinct permutation with this quality unless  $\max A=f(i)<f(i+1)=\min B$ , which occurs only when  $A$  is the first  $i$  elements of  $S$  for any given  $i$ , or  $n+1$  sets total. Our total is therefore  $2^n-(n+1)$ , so our final answer is (1), as desired.

stem_md: Let $f,g\colon [0,1]\to [0,1]$ be two functions such that $g$ is monotonic, surjective and $|f(x)-f(y)|\le |g(x)-g(y)|$ , for any $x,y\in [0,1]$ . [list]**a)** Prove that $f$ is continuous and that there exists some $x_0\in [0,1]$ with $f(x_0)=g(x_0)$ .**b)** Prove that the set $\{x\in [0,1]\, |\, f(x)=g(x)\}$ is a closed interval. [/list]
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>a)
Since  $g$  is continuous, we have:  $$  \lim_{y\to x} | f(x)-f(y)|\leq \lim_{y\to x} |g(x)-g(y)|=0  $$  therefore  $f$  is continuous.
WLOG assume  $g$  is nondecreasing.
Let  $h:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}$ ,  $h(x)=f(x)-g(x)$ , so  $h$  is continuous. Since  $g$  is monotone over a closed interval, it achieves a maximum and a minimum and because it is also surjective, we know that  $g(0)=0$  and  $g(1)=1$ . We know that  $h(0)\geq 0$ ,  $h(1)\leq 0$  and  $h$  continuous, therefore there exists  $x_0\in [0,1]$  such that  $h(x_0)=0$ , so  $f(x_0)=g(x_0)$ .

b)
WLOG assume  $g$  is nondecreasing.
Let  $x,y\in [0,1]$  with  $x>y$ , since  $g$  is nondecreasing, we have:  $$  g(x)-g(y)\geq 0  $$    $$  g(x)-g(y)\geq | f(x)-f(y)| \geq f(x)-f(y)   $$    $$  g(x)-f(x) \geq g(y)-f(y)  $$  thus  $h$  is also nondecreasing.
Let  $M=\{y\in [0,1] | h(y)=0\}$  and let  $y_0=\inf M$ ,  $z_0=\sup M$ . Since  $h$  is continuous,  $h(y_0)=h(z_0)=0$ . From the fact that  $h$  is monotone, we get that  $h(t)=0$  for all  $t\in [y_0,z_0]$ , therefore  $M=[y_0,z_0]$  as desired.</details>

stem_md: Let $n$ and $k$ be two natural numbers such that $n\ge 2$ and $1\le k\le n-1$ . Prove that if the matrix $A\in\mathcal{M}_n(\mathbb{C})$ has exactly $k$ minors of order $n-1$ equal to $0$ , then $\det (A)\ne 0$ .
solution_md:
Let  $adj(A)$  be the adjugate of  $A$ . 
Assume that  $det(A)=0$ . Then the rank of  $adj(A)$  is  $0$  or  $1$ . 
There are at  at least  $n^2-n+1$   non-zero entries of  $adj(A)$ .
Thus  $adj(A)\not={0}$  and  $rank(adj(A))=1$ . Since  $k\geq{1}$ , there is at least one zero entry  $b_{ij}$  of  $adj(A)$ . Since each column of  $adj(A)$  is a non-zero vector ( $k\leq{n-1}$ ), the line  $(b_{ij})_j$  is zero and  $k\geq{n}$ , a contradiction.

stem_md: Find all differentiable functions $f\colon [0,\infty)\to [0,\infty)$ for which $f(0)=0$ and $f^{\prime}(x^2)=f(x)$ for any $x\in [0,\infty)$ .
solution_md:
$\forall x\geq 0$  :  $f'(x)=f'\left((\sqrt{x})^2\right)=f(\sqrt{x})\geq 0$  , so  $f'(x)\geq 0 \Rightarrow f\uparrow [0,+\infty)$ Let  $g(x)=e^{-x}f(x)\;,\;x\geq 0$ . $g'(x)=e^{-x}(f'(x)-f(x))$ .

For  $x\geq 1\Rightarrow x\geq \sqrt{x} \Rightarrow f(x)\geq f(\sqrt{x}) \Rightarrow f(x)\geq f'(x) \Rightarrow g'(x)\geq 0$ . 

For  $0\leq x\leq 1\Rightarrow x\leq \sqrt{x} \Rightarrow f(x)\leq f(\sqrt{x}) \Rightarrow f(x)\leq f'(x) \Rightarrow g'(x)\leq 0$ .

So  $g(x)\leq g(1)\iff f(x)\leq f(1)e^{x-1}\;\;\forall x\geq 0\;\;(1)$ .

From  $f'(x)=f(\sqrt{x})$  we have that  $f'$  is differentiable in  $(0,+\infty)$  with  $f''(x)=\dfrac{f'(\sqrt{x})}{2\sqrt{x}}\geq 0$  , so  $f$  is convex in  $[0,+\infty)$ .

The tangent on  $A (1, f (1))$  is  $e: y-f (1) = f '(1) (x-1)$ . But  $ f '(1) = f (1) $  so  $e: y = f (1) x $  and  $f(x)\geq f(1)x\;\;\forall x\geq 0\;\;(2)$ The grpaph of  $f$  for  $x\in[0,1]$  is under the  $OA:y=\dfrac{f(1)-f(0)}{1-0}x \iff y=f(1)x$  , so  $f(x)\leq f(1)x\;\forall\;\;x\in[0,1]\;\;(3)$ .

From  $(2)\;,\;(3)$  we have  $f(x)=f(1)x\;\;\forall x\in[0,1]$ .

But for  $x\in (0,1)$  :  $f'(x^2)=f(x)\iff f(1)=f(1)x \iff (x-1)f(1)=0 \overset{x\in(0,1)}{\iff} f(1)=0$ .

So  $(1)\Rightarrow 0 \leq f (x) \leq f (1)e^{x-1} \iff 0 \leq f (x) \leq 0 \iff f (x) = 0 \;, \; \forall x \geq 0 $ .

\begin{align*}h'(x)=f'(x)-\alpha_{n+1}\beta_{n+1}x^{\beta_{n+1}-1}f\left(x^{\gamma_{n+1}}\right)-\alpha_{n+1}x^{\beta_{n+1}}f'\left(x^{\gamma_{n+1}}\right)\gamma_{n+1}x^{\gamma_{n+1}-1}\leq 0\end{align*} because  $f'(x)-\alpha_{n+1}\beta_{n+1}x^{\beta_{n+1}-1}f\left(x^{\gamma_{n+1}}\right)=f(\sqrt{x})-\alpha_{n}\sqrt{x}^{\beta_{n}}f\left(\sqrt{x}^{\gamma_{n}}\right)\leq 0$  (inductive hypothesis) and also  $-\alpha_{n+1}x^{\beta_{n+1}}f'\left(x^{\gamma_{n+1}}\right)\gamma_{n+1}x^{\gamma_{n+1}-1}\leq 0$ .Therefore  $h$  is decreasing and  $h(0)=0$  so  $h(x)\leq 0$ .Thus the inequality holds for  $n+1$ .

stem_md: Let $f\colon [0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}$ be a continuous function such that $\int_0^nf(x)f(n-x)\ \text{d}x=\int_0^nf^2(x)\ \text{d}x$ , for any natural number $n\ge 1$ . Prove that $f$ is a periodic function.
solution_md: @above: If  $g$  is integrable on  $[a,b]$  and  $\int\limits_a^b g^2(x)\mathrm{d}x=0,$  but  $g$  is not necessary continuous, then  $g$  is not necessary the identically zero function. We can have, for example,  $g(x)=0,~\forall~x \in [a,b] \setminus \{c,d\},~g(c)=1,~g(d)=2.$ However, if  $g$  is continuous, then there exists  $G,$  an antiderivative of  $g^2.$  Since  $G' \ge 0$  it follows that  $G$  is increasing and since  $G(a)=G(b),$  it follows that  $G(x)=0,~\forall~x \in [a,b]$  and so  $g(x)=0,~\forall~x \in [a,b].$

stem_md: Let $(R,+,\cdot)$ be a ring and let $f$ be a surjective endomorphism of $R$ such that $[x,f(x)]=0$ for any $x\in R$ , where $[a,b]=ab-ba$ , $a,b\in R$ . Prove that: [list]**a)** $[x,f(y)]=[f(x),y]$ and $x[x,y]=f(x)[x,y]$ , for any $x,y\in R\ ;$ **b)** If $R$ is a division ring and $f$ is different from the identity function, then $R$ is commutative. [/list]
solution_md:
a)
\[
0=[x+y,f(x)+f(y)]=[x,f(x)]+[x,f(y)]+[y,f(x)]+[y,f(y)]=[x,f(y)]+[y,f(x)]\implies [x,f(y)]=[f(x),y]
\]
proves the first part. Since  $f$  is surjective, there exists  $z$  such that  $f(z)=y$ . Then
\[
x[x,y]=x[x,f(z)]=x[f(x),z]=[f(x),xz]=[x,f(xz)]=[x,f(x)y]=f(x)[x,y],
\]
where  $x[f(x),z]=[f(x),xz]$  and  $[x,f(x)y]=f(x)[x,y]$  follow from the fact that  $x$  and  $f(x)$  commute.  $\square$ b) If  $f(x)\neq x$ , from part a) we know that  $x[x,y]=f(x)[x,y]$  for all  $y\in R$ . If  $[x,y]$  is a unit we arrive at a contradiction. Hence  $[x,y]=0$  so  $x$  is central. Let  $A:=\{a\in R^\times\mid f(a)=a\}$  be a subgroup of  $R^\times$ . By the above,  $R\setminus A$  is a subset of  $Z:=Z(R^\times)$ .

Assume FTSOC there exists  $a\in R^\times\setminus Z\subseteq A$ . Since  $f$  is not the identity map, there exists an element  $x$  not fixed by it. Then  $ax\not\in A$  so  $ax\in Z$ . Since  $x\in Z$ , we have  $a\in Z$ , a contradiction. Thus  $Z=R^\times$ , so  $R$  is commutative.  $\square$

solution_md:
Let $\mathcal{C}$ be the set of integrable functions $f\colon [0,1]\to\mathbb{R}$ such that $0\le f(x)\le x$ for any $x\in [0,1]$ . Define the function $f\colon\mathcal{C}\to\mathbb{R}$ by \[V(f)=\int_0^1f^2(x)\ \text{d}x-(\int_0^1f(x)\ \text{d}x)^2\ ,\ f\in\mathcal{C}\ .\] Determine the following two sets: [list]**a)** $\{V(f_a)\, |\, 0\le a\le 1\}$ , where $f_a(x)=0$ , if $0\le x\le a$ and $f_a(x)=x$ , if $a
$(a)$ Simple calculation shows that $V(f_a)=\frac{1+6a^2-4a^3-3a^4}{12}$ which takes minimum and maximum values at $a=1$ and $a=\frac{\sqrt5-1}{2}$ , respectively. So by IVT \[\{V(f_a)\, |\, 0\le a\le 1\}=[0,\frac{5(3-\sqrt5)}{24}]\] $(b)$ The idea is hidden in part $(a)$ . First by Cauchy inequality we have, \[\int_0^1f^2(x)\ \text{d}x=(\int_0^1f^2(x)\ \text{d}x)(\int_0^11^2\ \text{d}x) \geq (\int_0^1f(x)\ \text{d}x)^2\] So $ V(f) \geq 0$ Now let $a=\frac{\sqrt5-1}{2}$ , so that $a^2+a-1=0$ . Then \begin{eqnarray} \int_0^1f^2(x)\ \text{d}x &\leq& \int_0^1xf(x)\ \text{d}x=\int_0^1(x-a)f(x)\ \text{d}x+a\int_0^1f(x)\ \text{d}x \nonumber &\leq& \int_a^1(x-a)f(x)\ \text{d}x+a\int_0^1f(x)\ \text{d}x \nonumber &\leq&\int_a^1(x-a)x\ \text{d}x+\frac{a^2}{4}+(\int_0^1f(x)\ \text{d}x)^2 \nonumber &=&\frac{4-6a+3a^2+2a^3}{12}+(\int_0^1f(x)\ \text{d}x)^2 \nonumber &=&\frac{(2a+1)(a^2+a-1)+5(1-a)}{12}+(\int_0^1f(x)\ \text{d}x)^2 \nonumber &=&\frac{5(3-\sqrt5)}{24}+(\int_0^1f(x)\ \text{d}x)^2 \nonumber \end{eqnarray} So $V(f) \leq \frac{5(3-\sqrt5)}{24}$ and $\{V(f)\, |\, f\in\mathcal{C}\}=[0,\frac{5(3-\sqrt5)}{24}]$

stem_md: Let $m$ and $n$ be two nonzero natural numbers. Determine the minimum number of distinct complex roots of the polynomial $\prod_{k=1}^m\, (f+k)$ , when $f$ covers the set of $n^{\text{th}}$ - degree polynomials with complex coefficients.
solution_md:
Let $m$ and $n$ be two nonzero natural numbers. Determine the minimum number of distinct complex roots of the polynomial $\prod_{k=1}^m\, (f+k)$ , when $f$ covers the set of $n^{\text{th}}$ - degree polynomials with complex coefficients.
Hope I understood problem correctly. First observe that no two polynomials $f+i$ and $f+j$ have a common root for $i \not=j$ . So if there is a repeated root it can only be repeated root of $f+i$ for some unique $i$ . Also we know that $k^{th}$ order root of $f+i$ is the $(k-1)^{th}$ order root of $f'$ . Now suppose $x_1,x_2,...x_t$ are the repeated roots of $\prod_{k=1}^m\, (f+k)$ , where $x_j$ has order $a_j$ . Since $deg(f')=n-1$ we have \[ (a_1-1)+(a_2-1)+...+(a_t-1) \leq n-1 \Longrightarrow a_1+a_2+...+a_t \leq n-1+t\] Then the number of distinct roots of $\prod_{k=1}^m\, (f+k)=nm-(a_1+a_2+...+a_t)+t \geq nm-(n-1+t)+t=n(m-1)+1$ Equality occurs for $f(x)=(x-1)^n-1$

stem_md: Let  $n_1,\ldots,n_k$  be positive integers, and define  $d_1=1$  and  $d_i=\frac{(n_1,\ldots,n_{i-1})}{(n_1,\ldots,n_{i})}$ , for  $i\in \{2,\ldots,k\}$ , where  $(m_1,\ldots,m_{\ell})$  denotes the greatest common divisor of the integers  $m_1,\ldots,m_{\ell}$ . Prove that the sums \[\sum_{i=1}^k a_in_i\] with  $a_i\in\{1,\ldots,d_i\}$  for  $i\in\{1,\ldots,k\}$  are mutually distinct  $\mod n_1$ .
solution_md:
I will assume  $d_i = \frac{\gcd(n_1,n_2,...,n_{i-1})}{\gcd(n_1,n_2,...,n_i)}$ . WLOG let  $\gcd(n_1,n_2,...,n_k) = 1$  (dividing every number by a constant clearly does not change the problem)

So let's prove this problem by induction on  $k$ . The base case of  $k=1$  is obviously true since there is only one sum  $a_1$ .
Suppose the problem holds for all  $k \le M-1$ . I claim it holds for  $k=M$  then.
To show this, first suppose  $d_M = 1$ . But then the problem is obviously true, because the sum is simply  $\sum_{i=1}^{M-1} a_in_i + n_M$  which are distinct modulo  $n_1$  by the inductive hypothesis on  $k=M-1$ .
Hence suppose  $d_M$  is not  $1$ . This means that since  $\gcd(n_1,n_2,...,n_k) = 1$ , we have  $\gcd(n_1,n_2,...,n_{k-1})$  is not one. Call the gcd  $z$ . Then our sum is: $z \sum_{i=1}^{M-1} \left ( \frac{n_i}{z} \right )a_i + a_Mn_M$  where  $1 \le d_M \le z$ .
Suppose two of these sums are equivalent modulo  $n_1$ . This means that  $z$  must divide their difference. As  $z$  divides the first terms, it follows we need  $z|(a_M - b_M)n_M$  where  $a_M, b_M$  are the coefficients on  $n_M$  in each summation. But as  $\gcd(z,n_M) = 1$  it follows  $z|(a_M - b_M) \implies a_M = b_M$ . Hence two summations are equivalent modulo  $n_1$  iff the summation of the first  $M-1$   $a_in_i$  terms are equivalent modulo  $n_1$ . However, by the inductive hypothesis this never happens and thus we are done.

stem_md: Let  $ABCD$  be a cyclic quadrilateral such that the triangles  $BCD$  and  $CDA$  are not equilateral. Prove that if the Simson line of  $A$  with respect to  $\triangle BCD$  is perpendicular to the Euler line of  $BCD$ , then the Simson line of  $B$  with respect to  $\triangle ACD$  is perpendicular to the Euler line of  $\triangle ACD$ .
solution_md:
A bit easy but beautiful  :love:  
Let  $H,O$  be the orthocenter and circumcenter.  
It is easy to see that two points  $P,Q \in (ABC)$  have parallel Simson lines  $\iff P=Q$ , hence  $A$  is fixed with respect to  $\triangle BCD$ .  
Note that it suffices to prove that  $A$  lies on the Jerabek hyperbola of  $\triangle BCD$  (since  $B$  would lie on the Jerabek hyperbola of  $\triangle ACD$ ). Let  $P$  be the antigonal conjugate of  $H$  with respect to the Jerabek hyperbola of  $\triangle BCD$ . Let  $P_1,P_2$  be the projections of  $P$  onto  $BC$  and  $BD$ . Then   $90^\circ-\angle BP_1P_2 = \angle PP_1P_2 = \angle PBP_2 = \angle PBO - \angle OBD 
= \angle BPO - \angle HBC = \angle BHO - \angle HBC$  $_\blacksquare$

stem_md: Let  $A$  and  $B$  be finite sets of real numbers and let  $x$  be an element of  $A+B$ . Prove that \[|A\cap (x-B)|\leq \frac{|A-B|^2}{|A+B|}\] where  $A+B=\{a+b: a\in A, b\in B\}$ ,  $x-B=\{x-b: b\in B\}$  and  $A-B=\{a-b: a\in A, b\in B\}$ .
solution_md: Let  $A'$  and  $B'$  are respectively subsets of  $A$  and  $B$  such that if  $a' \in A'$  and  $a'+b' = x$  such that  $b' \in B$  then  $b' \in B'$ . Then the inequality becomes   $|A',B'| |A+B| \le |A-B|^2$ . So  $|A',B'||A+B|$  counts the number of the set  $(a',b',t_{a,b})$ , where  $t_{a,b} \in A+B$  and  $a,b$  are unique pair in  $A$  and  $B$  respectively satisfying  $a+b= t$ . Now map this to the set  $(a'-b, a-b') \in (A-B)^2$ . Assume  $(a'' - b_0, a_0 - b'') = (a'-b, a-b')$ , then we have  $a_0+b_0 = a+b$  implying  $a_0 = a ; b_0 = b; a'= a''$  and  $b'= b''$ , so the map is one-one and we are done.

stem_md: Prove that a finite simple planar graph has an orientation so that every vertex has out-degree at most 3.
solution_md:
Oops, I thought of **dgrozev**'s approach but didn't see a way to complete the solution. 
Anyways, I think this inductive solution works: 

<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>I will induct on the number of vertices,  $n$ . Base cases are trivial. 

Add edges to the planar graph such that each finite face has  $3$  edges. If we can prove the result for these graphs, then the result holds for all graphs. From adding the edges to our graph, we can see that if a vertex  $v$  has neighbors  $v_1, \cdots v_k$ , such that the edges between  $v$  and  $v_1, \cdots v_k$  are in clockwise order, then  $v_1v_2, v_2v_3, \cdots v_{k - 1} v_{k}$  are edges. Furthermore, we can add the edge  $v_1v_k$  if it does not already exist without contradicting planarity. (1)

Since the number of edges is at most  $3n - 6$ , there is at least one vertex with degree 5 or less. Call this vertex  $u$ . **Case 1:**  $d(u) \le 3$ Then we can just orient all edges of  $u$  outwards and apply the inductive hypothesis. **Case 2:**  $d(u) = 4$ Let vertex  $u$  have neighbors  $v_1, \cdots v_4$ . Delete vertex  $u$ , and add edge  $v_1v_3$  (since  $v_1 \cdots v_4$  are a face by (1), we can do this without contradicting planarity). Now apply the inductive hypothesis, and WLOG assume that  $v_1$  points towards  $v_3$ . Then have  $u$  point towards  $v_2$ ,  $v_4$ , and  $v_3$ , and  $v_1$  point towards  $u$ . **Case 3:**  $d(u) = 5$ Again delete  $u$  and add  $v_1v_3$  and  $v_1v_4$ . Apply the inductive hypothesis. 
If  $v_1v_3$  and  $v_1v_4$  both point towards  $v_1$ , then have  $v_3$  and  $v_4$  point towards  $u$ , and  $u$  point towards  $v_2, v_1, v_5$ . 
If  $v_1v_3$  point towards  $v_1$  but  $v_1v_4$  points towards  $v_4$ , then have  $v_3$  and  $v_1$  point towards  $u$  and  $u$  point towards  $v_4$ ,  $v_2$ ,  $v_5$ . 
If  $v_1$  points towards  $v_3$  and  $v_4$ , then at least one of  $v_2, v_5$  points towards  $v_1$ . Assume that  $v_2$  points towards  $v_1$ . Then switch the direction of  $v_1v_2$ , have  $u$  point towards  $v_3$ ,  $v_4$ ,  $v_5$ , and have  $v_1$  and  $v_2$  points towards  $u$ .

We will use the well known fact that every simple planar graph with  $n$  vertices has at most  $3n-6$  edges.
Let begin to orient consecutively the graph  $G$ . If an edge  $\{u,v\} \in E(G)$  we choose arbitrary the direction of this edge  $(u,v)$  or  $(v,u)$  complying the rule every vertex to has out-degree at most  $3$ .
We will stop in two cases:
1. There are no remaining edges to be oriented. In this case we are done.
2. We can not orient any of the remaining non oriented edges obeying the rule out-degrees to be at most  $3$ .
Let  $\{a,b\} \in E(G)$  is yet non oriented. Denote by  $d^o(a)$  the out-degree of  $a$ . Then  $d^o(a)=3$ , because if  $d^o(a)<3$  we can continue the process and orient  $\{a,b\}$  as  $(a,b)$ .
Let denote by  $O(a)$  all three vertices  $v_1,v_2,v_3$  corresponding to the oriented edges  $(a,v_1),(a,v_2),(a,v_3)$ . More generally, if  $V \subset V(G)$ , denote by  $O(V)$  all  $u \in G$  such that there exists  $v\in V$  for which  $(v,u)$  is oriented in such way. 
Let now  $O^2(a)=O(O(a)),\ldots, O^n(a)=O(O^{n-1}(a))$ . Assume that for some  $n$ , there exists  $v \in O^n(a)$  such that  $d^o(v) < 3$ . Then there will be  a sequence of oriented edges  $(a,v_1),(v_1,v_2),(v_2,v_3),\ldots,(v_{\ell}, v) $ . Then we can change these oriented edges with their opposite derections, i.e.  $(v_1,a),(v_2,v_1),(v_3,v_2),\ldots,(v, v_{\ell})$  and in that way the new oriented graph will have  $d^o(a)=2$ , so we can continue the above process by orienting  $\{a,b\}$  as  $(a,b)$ .
Let now assume that  $\forall n, \, \forall v \in O^n(a),\,  d^o(v)=3$ . Denote by  $G_1$  the oriented graph with  $V(G_1)= \{a\} \cup \bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty} O^i(a) $  and  $E(G_1)$  be all oriented edges connecting vertices of  $V(G_1)$ .
Obviously  $G_1$  is a planar graph as a subgraph of  $G$ . With current assumptions  $\forall v \in V(G_1),\, d^o_{G_1}(v)=3$ . This means  $E(G_1)=3 V(G_1)$ . Thus  $G_1$  is not a planar graph, contradiction.

stem_md:
Let  $p$  and  $q$  be two given positive integers. A set of  $p+q$  real numbers  $a_1<a_2<\cdots <a_{p+q}$  is said to be balanced iff  $a_1,\ldots,a_p$  were an arithmetic progression with common difference  $q$  and  $a_p,\ldots,a_{p+q}$  where an arithmetic progression with common difference  $p$ . Find the maximum possible number of balanced sets, so that any two of them have nonempty intersection. 

Comment: The intended problem also had " $p$  and  $q$  are coprime" in the hypothesis. A typo when the problems where written made it appear like that in the exam (as if it were the only typo in the olympiad). Fortunately, the problem can be solved even if we didn't suppose that and it can be further generalized: we may suppose that a balanced set has  $m+n$  reals  $a_1<\cdots <a_{m+n-1}$  so that  $a_1,\ldots,a_m$  is an arithmetic progression with common difference  $p$  and  $a_m,\ldots,a_{m+n-1}$  is an arithmetic progression with common difference  $q$ .
solution_md:
I only give the proof when  $p,q$  is co-prime.
The answer is  $p+\max\{p,q\}$ .
The case when  $p\ge q$  is trivial.
As for the case  $p<q$ , the construction is trivial, too.
Define  $0=x_1<x_2<\ldots<x_k$  are all minimal elements in each balanced set. It's not hard to prove for any incidences  $i<j$ , there is unique pair of integers  $0\le u\le q,0\le v\le p-1$  such that  $x_j-x_i=up+vq$ .
Specifically, we have  $x_i=x_i-x_1=u_i p+v_i q$ (where  $u_i,v_i$  are defined before). Easy to prove   $$ 0=u_1+v_1<u_2+v_2<\ldots<u_k+v_k $$  Since above are all integer,we get  $u_k+v_k\ge k-1$ .
Thus   $$ 2pq-q\ge x_k\ge u_k p+(k-1-u_k)q=(k-1)q-u_k(q-p)\ge (k-1)q-q(q-p)\implies k\le p+q $$

stem_md: Prove that for any positive integer  $n\geq 2$  we have that \[\sum_{k=2}^n \lfloor \sqrt[k]{n}\rfloor=\sum_{k=2}^n\lfloor\log_{k}n\rfloor.\]
solution_md:
We prove the desired result by induction.
First, the base case which is  $n = 2$ . Then we have  $\lfloor\sqrt{2}\rfloor = \lfloor\log_{2} 2\rfloor = 1$ , so our base case is proven.
Next, for the inductive step. Assume that   $$ \sum_{k=2}^n \lfloor \sqrt[k]{n}\rfloor=\sum_{k=2}^n\lfloor\log_{k}n\rfloor $$   is true for  $n$ . We prove it is true for  $n+1$ .
Observe that  $\lfloor\sqrt[k]{n}\rfloor$  can only increase by  $1$  when  $n$  is a perfect  $kth$  power. Similarly,  $\lfloor \log_{k} n\rfloor$  can only increase by  $1$  when  $n$  is a power of  $k$ . For all the  $\lfloor \sqrt[k]{n+1}\rfloor$  which increases by  $1$  from  $\lfloor \sqrt[k]{n}\rfloor$ , because  $n+1 = c^{k}$  for some  $c$  we have  $\lfloor\log_{c} n\rfloor$  increase by  $1$  as well. This implies a bijection for all  $\lfloor\sqrt[k]{n}\rfloor$  that increase by  $1$  to all  $\lfloor\log_{k}n\rfloor$  that increase by  $1$ , therefore   $$ \sum_{k=2}^{n+1} \lfloor \sqrt[k]{n+1}\rfloor=\sum_{k=2}^{n+1}\lfloor\log_{k}n+1\rfloor $$   is true as well.
Our induction is complete, so we know that it is true for all  $n$ .

Let  $S$  be the set of all ordered pairs  $(a,b)$  of positive integers greater than  $1$  such that  $a^b \leq n$ . We count the number of elements of  $S$  in two ways.

First, consider all solutions to  $a^b \leq n$  for a fixed  $a$ . This is equivalent to  $ b \leq \log_a n$ , so there are  $\lfloor \log_a n \rfloor - 1$  solutions for each  $a$  from 2 to  $n$ . Then consider all solutions to  $a^b \leq n$  for a fixed  $b$ . This is equivalent to  $a \leq \sqrt[b]{n}$ , so there are  $\lfloor \sqrt[b]{n} \rfloor - 1$  solutions for each  $b$  from 2 to  $n$ .

Summing up over all  $a$  and all  $b$  for each counting method shows
\[\sum_{k=2}^n (\lfloor \sqrt[k]{n} \rfloor - 1) = \sum_{k=2}^n (\lfloor \log_k n \rfloor - 1),\]
which is equivalent to what we want.

Shorter, given a boolean predicate  $\mathcal{P}$ , we shall use the notation popularized by D. Knuth  $[[\mathcal{P}]] =1$  if  $\mathcal{P}$  is true, while  $[[\mathcal{P}]]=0$  if  $\mathcal{P}$  is false.
Then  $\displaystyle \sum_{k=2}^n \left \lfloor \sqrt[k]{n}\right \rfloor =\sum_{k=2}^n \Big ( 1+\sum_{\ell=2}^n [[\ell^{k} \leq n]] \Big ) = \sum_{\ell=2}^n \Big ( 1+\sum_{k=2}^n [[\ell^{k} \leq n]] \Big ) = \sum_{\ell=2}^n \left \lfloor \log_{\ell} n \right \rfloor$ .

stem_md: Let  $k$  be a positive integer. Find the maximum value of \[a^{3k-1}b+b^{3k-1}c+c^{3k-1}a+k^2a^kb^kc^k,\] where  $a$ ,  $b$ ,  $c$  are non-negative reals such that  $a+b+c=3k$ .
solution_md:
This inequality is generalization of a well known one:  $a^2b+b^2c+c^2a+abc \leq \frac{4}{27}(a+b+c)^3$ and it can be proved in the same way, so in my opinion, it's not the best choice for such an important tst..


This is my proof (basically the same as mavropnevma proof with few things explained more):

WLOG we can suppose that  $a=max \{a,b,c \}$ . We can see that for  $a\ge b\ge c$  we have:  $a^n b +b^n c+ c^n a \geq ab^n+bc^n+ca^n$ , so we can suppose that  $a\ge b\ge c$ .

Denote now  $f(a,b,c)=a^{3k-1}b+b^{3k-1}c+c^{3k-1}a + k^2 a^kb^kc^k$ We want to prove that  $f(a,b,c) \leq f(a+c,b,0)$ , what is equal to: $(a+c)^{3k-1}b \geq a^{3k-1}b+b^{3k-1}c+c^{3k-1}a + k^2 a^kb^kc^k \quad (1)$ We can see that when we expand LHS, we will have: $a^{3k-1}b+a^{3k-2}bc+(3k-2)a^{3k-2}bc+ \dbinom{3k-1}{2} a^{3k-3}bc^2+ ...+(3k-1)c^{3k-2}ab$ Now we can see that for  $k=1$ ,  $(1)$  follows from first three and the last summands, and for  $k\ge 2$ ,  $(1)$  follows from the first four summands because  $\dbinom{3k-1}{2} \geq k^2$ .

Hence, maximum is reached when  $c=0$ , and it is equal to  $f(a,b,c) \leq (3k-1)^{3k-1}$ , what mavropnevma showed.

Equality holds for  $k=1$  when  $(a,b,c)=(1,1,1)$  or  $(2,1,0)$  and for  $k\ge 2$  when  $(a,b,c)=(3k-1,1,0)$  with cyclic permutations.  $\blacksquare$

stem_md: Let  $m$  and  $n$  be two positive integers greater than  $1$ . Prove that there are  $m$  positive integers  $N_1$  ,  $\ldots$  ,  $N_m$  (some of them may be equal) such that \[\sqrt{m}=\sum_{i=1}^m{(\sqrt{N_i}-\sqrt{N_i-1})^{\frac{1}{n}}.}\]
solution_md:
Using the subtraction version of the **Groovy number theorem**:

*Call a number groovy if it is of the form  $\sqrt {n+1}-\sqrt{n}$  for some positive integer  $n$ . Then if  $x$  is groovy, then  $x^r$  is groovy for all positive integers  $r$ .* (See 2009 USAMTS Round 1, problem 5 for the proof)

we can write  $\sqrt m=(\sqrt 1-\sqrt 0)+(\sqrt 2-\sqrt 1)+(\sqrt 3-\sqrt 2)+\dots+(\sqrt m-\sqrt{m-1})$  and we're done, since each  $\sqrt {i}-\sqrt {i-1}$  can be expressed as the  $n$ th root of  $\sqrt{N_i}-\sqrt{N_i-1}$  for some  $N_i$ .

stem_md: Let  $a_1$  ,  $\ldots$  ,  $a_n$  be positive integers and  $a$  a positive integer that is greater than  $1$  and is divisible by the product  $a_1a_2\ldots a_n$ . Prove that  $a^{n+1}+a-1$  is not divisible by the product  $(a+a_1-1)(a+a_2-1)\ldots(a+a_n-1)$ .
solution_md:
Suppose the opposite is true and let  $P(x)=x^{n+1}+x-1-k\prod_{i=1}^n(x+a_i-1)$  where  $k\in \mathbb{Z}$  and  $P(a)=0$ .
Let  $P(x)=(x-a)\cdot Q(x)$ . $P(1)\equiv 1\pmod{\prod_{i=1}^n a_i}$  and hence as  $1-a\equiv 1\pmod{\prod_{i=1}^n a_i}$   $\implies$   $Q(1)\equiv 1\pmod{\prod_{i=1}^n a_i}$ . $|Q(1)|= \frac{\mid k\prod_{i=1}^n a_i-1\mid}{\mid a-1\mid} $ .Note that if all  $a_1,a_2,...a_n$  are one than we have that  $a\mid 1$  contradiction as  $a\not =1$   $\implies$   $$ 0=a^{n+1}+a-1-k\prod_{i=1}^n (a+a_i-1)\leq a^{n+1}+a-1-k \cdot a^{n-1}(a+1) $$  And so if  $k\geq a$  we would have that  $-1\geq 0$ ,impossible and so  $k\leq a-1$   $\implies$   $|Q(1)|\geq \prod_{i=1}^n a_i$  and hence as  $Q(1)\equiv 1\pmod{\prod_{i=1}^n a_i}$   $\implies$   $Q(1)=1$   $\implies$   $P(1)=1-a$  and hence  $a=k\prod_{i=1}^n a_i$  but as  $k\mid a$  and  $P(a)=0$   $\implies$   $k\mid -1$   $\implies$   $k=1$  (everything is positive after all).However  $a\mid \prod_{i=1}^{n}(a_i-1)+1$  by rational root theorem but the left side is larger than the right and hence a contradiction. $\blacksquare$

stem_md: Let  $S$  be a set of positive integers, each of them having exactly  $100$  digits in base  $10$  representation. An element of  $S$  is called *atom* if it is not divisible by the sum of any two (not necessarily distinct) elements of  $S$ . If  $S$  contains at most  $10$  atoms, at most how many elements can  $S$  have?
solution_md:
<u>Sketch</u>. $S$  has  $10$  atoms, because otherwise we could add some  $100$ -digit number to  $S$  and increase the number of elements in  $S$ .

Let  $A = \{a_1,\ldots,a_{10}\} \subseteq S$  be the set of  $10$  atoms. By induction it can be shown that every element  $s \in S$  can be expressed as a linear combination  $s = \lambda_1a_1+\lambda_2a_2+\cdots +\lambda_{10}a_{10}$ , for integers  $0\le \lambda_i \le 9$  and  $1 \le \lambda_1+ \cdots +\lambda_{10} \le 9$ . Furthermore, if  $S$  is maximal then every such linear combination must be an element of  $S$ .

So enumerating all the possible vectors  $(\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\ldots,\lambda_{10})$  by a ball-and-urn argument gives an upper bound of  $\binom{9+10}{9} - 1$ .

This can be achieved by defining  $a_i = 10^{99} + 2^{i-1}$  for  $i= 1,2,\ldots,10$ , and setting  $S$  equal to all linear combinations of the  $a_i$ .

solution_md: First Consider a other triangle  $A'B'C'$  in a complex plane. Let  $C'$  be the origin and  $A'=a,B'=b,D'=z_1,E'=z_2$ Now easy to determine  $z_1=\frac {b|a|}{|a|+|a-b|}$  and  $z_2=\frac {a|b|}{|b|+|a-b|}$ Now letting  $a=1$  we've  $z_1-z_2=\frac {b}{1+|1-b|}-\frac {|b|}{|b|+|1-b|}$ Now suppose  $|B|=1$  then we get | $z_1-z_2|=|\frac {b-1}{1+|1-b|}|$ So in this case now it's same as to show  $\frac{2}{|b-1|}+|b-1|\geq 2\sqrt2$ .... direct from  $AM-GM$ Now so we need to look for case when triangle is not isosceles. Now it's clear that if  $P,Q$  be points on  $AB$  beyond  $B$  and on  $AC$  beyond  $C$  then  $PQ>BC$ . Now after proving for the case isosceles consider the triangle now if we don't have  $\angle {3C+2A}<180^0 $  or  $\angle {3C+2B}<180^0 $  then not done directly , but since one of them is false so done.

stem_md: Let  $f, g:\mathbb{Z}\rightarrow [0,\infty )$  be two functions such that  $f(n)=g(n)=0$  with the exception of finitely many integers  $n$ . Define  $h:\mathbb{Z}\rightarrow [0,\infty )$  by \[h(n)=\max \{f(n-k)g(k): k\in\mathbb{Z}\}.\] Let  $p$  and  $q$  be two positive reals such that  $1/p+1/q=1$ . Prove that \[ \sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}h(n)\geq \Bigg(\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}f(n)^p\Bigg)^{1/p}\Bigg(\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}g(n)^q\Bigg)^{1/q}.\]
solution_md:
Let  $S$  is finite,  $S \subset \mathbb{Z}$  and  $f(n)=g(n)=0,\, n \in \mathbb{Z} \setminus S$ . 
We use a standart notation  $\|f\|_{p} = \left( \sum_{i\in S} |f(i)|^p \right)^{\frac{1}{p}}, p < \infty;\, \|f\|_{\infty} = \max_{i\in S}|f(i)| $ . We have:

(1)  $ \sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}h(n) \geq \|f\|_{\infty} \|g\|_1 $ .

Why? If  $\|f\|_{\infty} = f(n_0) \, \Rightarrow \, h(n_0 + n) \geq \|f\|_{\infty} g(n)$  and summing up we get (1).

In the same way:
(2)  $ \sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}h(n) \geq \|g\|_{\infty} \|f\|_1 $ .

From (1) and (2) follows:

(3)  $ \sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}h(n) \geq \frac{1}{q} \|f\|_{\infty} \|g\|_1 + \frac{1}{p} \|g\|_{\infty} \|f\|_1 $ .

Now we write: $\sum_{n\in S} f(n)^p \leq \|f\|_{\infty}^{p-1}\|f\|_1$ , which implies:

(4)  $ \|f\|_{\infty}^{\frac{1}{q}} \|f\|_1^{\frac{1}{p}} \geq \|f\|_p $ .

(5)  $\|g\|_{\infty}^{\frac{1}{p}} \|g\|_1^{\frac{1}{q}} \geq \|g\|_q $ .

Multiplying (4) and (5) we get:

(6)  $ \left( \|f\|_{\infty} \|g\|_1 \right)^{\frac{1}{q}} \left( \|g\|_{\infty} \|f\|_1 \right)^{\frac{1}{p}} \geq \|f\|_p \|g\|_q $ .

Now, (3) , (6) and weighted AM-GM imply: $ \sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}h(n) \geq  \|f\|_p \|g\|_q $ .

Comment. The fact that  $f,g$  vanish with the exception of finitely many integers is not so essential. Slightly restating the problem we can get rid of that requirement.
