<details><summary>Solution - grinding USAMO problems</summary>$$ \color{red} \spadesuit\color{red} \boxed{\textbf{Solution.}}\color{red} \spadesuit $$  By Menelaus, the desired is equivalent to proving that  $$ \frac{AB'}{A'B}+\frac{BC'}{B'C}+\frac{CA'}{C'A}=1. $$  Letting  $\angle BA'P=\alpha, \angle CB'P=\beta, \angle AC'P = \gamma$  and applying Law of sines three times, this is equivalent to  $$ \frac{AP}{BP}\cdot \frac{\sin \alpha}{\sin \beta} \cdot \frac{BP}{CP}\cdot \frac{\sin \beta}{\sin \gamma} \cdot \frac{CP}{AP}\cdot \frac{\sin \gamma}{\sin \alpha}=1, $$  which is obviously true.</details>

Observe that angle A'PC=APC', and same for the other symmetrical angles. 

Then by law of sines, A'C/sin(A'PC)=A'P/sin(A'CP). Similarly, AC'/sin(APC')=C'P/sin(C'AP). 

Divide the two equations to get A'C/AC'=A'Psin(C'AP)/C'Psin(A'CP)=A'Psin(BAP)/C'Psin(BCP). 

Get symmetrical expressions for B'A/BA' and C'B/CB', and multiply them together. You're left with 6 sines, 3 on top and 3 on bottom. 

Multiply top and bottom by PA*PB*PC. Use Law of Sines again, using triangles PAB, PAC, and PBC, and you can finish with Menelaus's Theorem.

Set  $P$  as the origin and rotate the figure so that  $\gamma$  is the y-axis. Then let  $A = (x_1, y_1), B = (x_2, y_2), C = (x_3,y_3)$ .
Remark that  $PA$  reflect across  $\gamma$  is simply the line  $y = -(y_1/x_1)x$ .
We need this to hit  $BC$ .  $BC$ 's slope is  $\frac{y_3-y_2}{x_3-x_2}$  and so the line  $BC$  is represented by  $y = \frac{y_3-y_2}{x_3-x_2}x + y_2 - \frac{y_3-y_2}{x_3-x_2}x_2$ Equating these, we find  $\left ( \frac{y_2 - y_3}{x_3 - x_2} - \frac{y_1}{x_1} \right )x = y_2 - \frac{y_3 - y_2}{x_3 - x_2}x_2$  $\implies x = \frac{y_2(x_3 - x_2)x_1 - (y_3-y_2)x_1x_2}{x_1(y_2 - y_3) - y_1(x_3 - x_2)}$  $ = \frac{y_2x_1x_3 - y_2x_2x_1 - y_3x_1x_2 +  y_2x_1x_2}{x_1y_2 - x_1y_3 - y_1x_3 + y_1x_2}$  $ = \frac{y_2x_1x_3 - y_3x_1x_2}{x_1y_2 - x_1y_3 - y_1x_3 + y_1x_2}$ Hence  $A' = \left ( \frac{y_2x_1x_3 - y_3x_1x_2}{x_1y_2 - x_1y_3 - y_1x_3 + y_1x_2}, -\frac{y_1(y_2x_3 - y_3x_2)}{x_1y_2 - x_1y_3 - y_1x_3 + y_1x_2} \right )$ By permuting the variables we get: $B' = \left ( \frac{y_1x_2x_3 - y_3x_2x_1}{x_2y_1 - x_2y_3 - y_2x_3 + y_2x_1}, -\frac{y_2(y_1x_3 - y_3x_1)}{x_2y_1 - x_2y_3 - y_2x_3 + y_2x_1} \right )$  $C' = \left ( \frac{y_1x_3x_2 - y_2x_3x_1}{x_3y_1 - x_3y_2 - y_3x_2 + y_3x_1}, -\frac{y_3(y_1x_2 - y_2x_1)}{x_3y_1 - x_3y_2 - y_3x_2 + y_3x_1} \right )$ Now to show  $A',B',C'$  are collinear it suffices to show  $C' - B'$  has the same slope as  $C'-A'$ .
C' - B' = \left ( \frac{y_1x_3x_2 - y_2x_3x_1}{x_3y_1 - x_3y_2 - y_3x_2 + y_3x_1} - \frac{y_1x_2x_3 - y_3x_2x_1}{x_2y_1 - x_2y_3 - y_2x_3 + y_2x_1}, \frac{y_2(y_1x_3 - y_3x_1)}{x_2y_1 - x_2y_3 - y_2x_3 + y_2x_1} - \frac{y_3(y_1x_2 - y_2x_1)}{x_3y_1 - x_3y_2 - y_3x_2 + y_3x_1} \right )
(LaTeX tags taken away so it displays)
C' - A' = \left ( \frac{y_1x_3x_2 - y_2x_3x_1}{x_3y_1 - x_3y_2 - y_3x_2 + y_3x_1} - \frac{y_2x_1x_3 - y_3x_1x_2}{x_1y_2 - x_1y_3 - y_1x_3 + y_1x_2}, \frac{y_1(y_2x_3 - y_3x_2)}{x_1y_2 - x_1y_3 - y_1x_3 + y_1x_2} - \frac{y_3(y_1x_2 - y_2x_1)}{x_3y_1 - x_3y_2 - y_3x_2 + y_3x_1} \right )

Hence we will be done if we can show:
\frac{\frac{y_1(y_2x_3 - y_3x_2)}{x_1y_2 - x_1y_3 - y_1x_3 + y_1x_2} - \frac{y_3(y_1x_2 - y_2x_1)}{x_3y_1 - x_3y_2 - y_3x_2 + y_3x_1}}{\frac{y_1x_3x_2 - y_2x_3x_1}{x_3y_1 - x_3y_2 - y_3x_2 + y_3x_1} - \frac{y_2x_1x_3 - y_3x_1x_2}{x_1y_2 - x_1y_3 - y_1x_3 + y_1x_2}} = \frac{\frac{y_2(y_1x_3 - y_3x_1)}{x_2y_1 - x_2y_3 - y_2x_3 + y_2x_1} - \frac{y_3(y_1x_2 - y_2x_1)}{x_3y_1 - x_3y_2 - y_3x_2 + y_3x_1}}{\frac{y_1x_3x_2 - y_2x_3x_1}{x_3y_1 - x_3y_2 - y_3x_2 + y_3x_1} - \frac{y_1x_2x_3 - y_3x_2x_1}{x_2y_1 - x_2y_3 - y_2x_3 + y_2x_1}}

Remark that the LHS is simply: $\frac{ y_1(y_2x_3 - y_3x_2)(x_3y_1 - x_3y_2 - y_3x_2 + y_3x_1) - y_3(y_1x_2 - y_2x_1)(x_1y_2 - x_1y_3 - y_1x_3 + y_1x_2)}{(y_1x_3x_2 - y_2x_3x_1)(x_1y_2 - x_1y_3 - y_1x_3 + y_1x_2) - (y_2x_1x_3 - y_3x_1x_2)(x_3y_1 - x_3y_2 - y_3x_2 + y_3x_1)}$ while the RHS is: $\frac{ y_2(y_1x_3 - y_3x_1)(x_3y_1 - x_3y_2 - y_3x_2 + y_3x_1) - y_3(y_1x_2 - y_2x_1)(x_2y_1 - x_2y_3 - y_2x_3 + y_2x_1)}{ (y_1x_3x_2 - y_2x_3x_1)(x_2y_1 - x_2y_3 - y_2x_3 + y_2x_1) - (y_1x_2x_3 - y_3x_2x_1)(x_3y_1 - x_3y_2 - y_3x_2 + y_3x_1) }$ AND HUZZAH THE NUMERATORS AND DENOMINATORS ARE THE SAME AFTER EXPANSION! There is one configuration issue; one of the angles is  $0^{\circ}$ . This forces  $P$  to lie on one of the sides of  $\triangle ABC$  (WLOG this side is  $AC$ ), so that  $P\equiv B'$ . But then we have  $PA\equiv PC$ , so the three points are trivially collinear.

Thus, we're done $.\:\blacksquare\:$

We will prove the following more general result:

Let  $\ell_1$  and  $\ell_2$  be lines in the plane of  $ABC$  that intersect at  $P$ . The harmonic conjugate of line  $PA$  with respect to  $\ell_1$  and  $\ell_2$  intersects  $BC$  at  $A'$ , and  $B'$  and  $C'$  are defined similarly. Then,  $A'$ ,  $B'$ , and  $C'$  are collinear.

Note that the result is purely projective, so take a projective transformation that takes  $P$  to some point at infinity. Project all of this through  $P$  onto some arbitrary line  $\ell$ . By Menelaus, this now becomes the following:

Let  $P_1,P_2,A,B,C$  be five collinear points. Let  $A',B',C'$  be the harmonic conjugates of  $A,B,C$  with respect to  $P_1$  and  $P_2$ . Then,  $\frac{A'B}{A'C}\cdot\frac{B'C}{B'A}\cdot\frac{C'A}{C'B}=1$ . Now we proceed using real numbers. Set  $p_1=-1$  and  $p_2=1$ . Note that  $a'=\frac{1}{a}$ ,  $b'=\frac{1}{b}$ , and  $c'=\frac{1}{c}$ . But now we have  $\frac{\frac1a-b}{\frac1a-c}\cdot\frac{\frac1b-c}{\frac1b-a}\cdot\frac{\frac1c-a}{\frac1c-b}=\frac{1-ab}{1-ac}\cdot\frac{1-bc}{1-ba}\cdot\frac{1-ca}{1-cb}=1$  as desired.

Back to the original problem, let  $\gamma'$  be the line through  $P$  perpendicular to  $\gamma$ . It is well known that  $(\gamma,\gamma';PA,PA')=-1$ , so by applying our generalized result we are done.

What a cute algebra problem. We complex bash. Set $\gamma$ as the real axis. Also without loss of generality shift till $p = 0$ . Then take $a$ , $b$ and $c$ as free variables. Let $D = \overline{AP} \cap \overline{BC}$ . Similarly define $E$ and $F$ . Computing $d$ we find, \begin{align*} d = \frac{ - a(\overline{b}c - b\overline{c})}{\overline{a}(b-c) - a(\overline{b}-\overline{c})} \end{align*} Okay that wasn't too bad. Now similarly we can compute, \begin{align*} e &= \frac{- b(\overline{c}a - c\overline{a})}{\overline{b}(c-a) - b(\overline{c} - \overline{a})} f &= \frac{- c(\overline{a}b - a\overline{b})}{\overline{c}(a-b) - c(\overline{a}-\overline{b})} \end{align*} Note that $A'$ , $B'$ and $C'$ are just reflections over the real axis of $D$ , $E$ and $F$ so it suffices to show that $D$ , $E$ and $F$ are collinear. To show this it suffices to show, \begin{align*} 0 &= \begin{vmatrix} d & \overline{d} & 1 e & \overline{e} &1 f & \overline{f} & 1 \end{vmatrix} &= \begin{vmatrix} \frac{ - a(\overline{b}c - b\overline{c})}{(\overline{a}b - a\overline{b}) - (\overline{a}c - a\overline{c})} & \frac{ -\overline{a}(\overline{b}c - b\overline{c} )}{(\overline{a}b - a\overline{b}) - (\overline{a}c - a\overline{c})} & 1 \frac{ -b(\overline{c}a - c\overline{a})}{ (\overline{b}c - b\overline{c}) - (\overline{b}a - b\overline{a}) } & \frac{-\overline{b}(\overline{c}a - c\overline{a})}{ (\overline{b}c - b\overline{c}) - (\overline{b}a - b\overline{a})} &1 \frac{-c(\overline{a}b - a\overline{b})}{(\overline{c}a -c\overline{a}) - (\overline{c}b - c\overline{b})} & \frac{-\overline{c}(\overline{a}b - a\overline{b}}{(\overline{c}a -c\overline{a}) - (\overline{c}b - c\overline{b})} & 1 \end{vmatrix} \end{align*} Then it suffices to show that, \begin{align*} 0 &= \begin{vmatrix} a & \overline{a} & \frac{(\overline{a}b - a\overline{b}) - (\overline{a}c - a\overline{c})}{(\overline{b}c - b\overline{c})} b & \overline{b} & \frac{(\overline{b}c - b\overline{c}) - (\overline{b}a - b\overline{a})}{(\overline{c}a - c\overline{a})} c & \overline{c} & \frac{(\overline{c}a -c\overline{a}) - (\overline{c}b - c\overline{b})}{ (\overline{a}b - a\overline{b})} \end{vmatrix} \end{align*} Now we expand by minors to find, \begin{align*} \sum_{cyc} \frac{(\overline{c}a -c\overline{a}) - (\overline{c}b - c\overline{b})}{ (\overline{a}b - a\overline{b})} \cdot (a\overline{b} - \overline{a}b) &= \sum_{cyc} -\overline{c}a + c\overline{a} + \overline{c}b - c\overline{b} &= 0 \end{align*} and we're done.

Let \[ T(a,b) = \{1\le k <2012:ak\%2012>bk\%2012\}. \] We want to minimize $|T(a,b)|$ over all $1\le a\not = b \le 2011$ . -------- **Lemma:**For any integer $x$ and any integer $m$ , we have \[ (2012m-x)\% 2012= \begin{cases} 2012-(x\% 2012) &\text{if } 2012\nmid x 0&\text{if } 2012\mid x. \end{cases}\] *Proof:* Obvious. The reason for the discrepancy is that remainders upon dividing by $2012$ cannot be $2012$ , they must be less! $\blacksquare$ **Claim: **For any $k\in [1,2011]$ : [list=1] [*] If $2012\mid (a-b)k$ or $2012\mid ak$ , then neither $k$ nor $2012-k$ is in $T(a,b)$ . [*] Else, exactly one of $k$ and $2012-k$ is in $T(a,b)$ . [/list] *Proof:*Assume $2012\nmid k(a-b)$ , i.e. $ak\% 2012\not = bk\% 2012$ . We have \[ 2012-k\in T(a,b)\iff (2012a-ak)\% 2012 > (2012b-bk)\% 2012. \quad (\clubsuit)\] By Lemma 1: - *Case 1:* $2012\nmid ak$ . Then \begin{align*} (\clubsuit) &\iff 2012-(ak\%2012)>2012-(bk\%2012) &\iff ak\% 2012\not > bk\% 2012 &\iff k\not \in T(a,b), \end{align*} the last step since we assumed $ak\% 2012\not = bk\% 2012$ . So in this case, $2012-k\in T(a,b) \iff k\not \in T(a,b)$ , i.e. exactly one of $k$ and $2012-k$ is in $T(a,b)$ . - *Case 2:* $2012\mid ak$ . Then we claim $k,2012-k\not \in T(a,b)$ . This is because $ak\% 2012=0$ , and $a(2012-k)\%2012=0$ too (not 2012; remainders are **less**than 2012!!!). $\blacksquare$ ----------- The conditions $2012\mid ka$ and $2012\mid k(a-b)$ are equivalent to $d_1\mid k$ and $d_2\mid k$ respectively, for some $d_1,d_2\mid 2012$ . (In particular, $d_1=\tfrac{2012}{\gcd(2012,a)}$ and $d_2=\tfrac{2012}{\gcd(2012,a-b)}$ .) So if $d_1\mid k$ or $d_2\mid k$ , then neither $k$ nor $2012-k$ are in $T(a,b)$ . In particular, now $d_1\mid k \iff d_1\mid 2012-k$ , so in each of the following pairs (and single 1006): \[ (1,2011),(2,2010),(3,2009),\ldots,(1005,1007),(1006),\] either both are in $T(a,b)$ or exactly one is. We want to minimize $|T(a,b)|$ , so we need to choose $a$ and $b$ to maximize the number of $k$ satisfying $d_1\mid k$ or $d_2\mid k$ . We cannot have $d_1$ or $d_2$ be 1, since we cannot have $2012\mid a$ or $2012\mid a-b$ since $a,b\in [1,2011]$ . We can have $d_2=2$ by $a-b=1006$ . So if $a-b=1006$ , then none of $2,4,6,\ldots,2010$ can be in $T(a,b)$ , and exactly one of each of \[ (1,2011),(3,2009),\ldots,(1005,1007)\] can be in $T(a,b)$ . So we have $503$ numbers in $T(a,b)$ ... But we still have $d_1$ to use! We should use $d_1=503$ to eliminate more than what we've already eliminated, since $2012=2^2\cdot 503$ , and using $d_2=2,4$ doesn't eliminate more than we already have with $d_1$ . If $d_1=503$ , then we further cannot have any of $(503,3\cdot 503)$ be in $T(a,b)$ . So when $d_1=503$ , i.e. $\gcd(2012,a)=4$ , we remove 1 more pair, which is the most we can remove (e.g. $d_1=4$ removes 0 pairs). So in fact the minimum is $\boxed{502}$ numbers in $T(a,b)$ . This is achieved when, e.g. $a=1008$ and $b=2$ .
RemarksThe main idea is the pairing, the rest is annoying details. The discrepancy of Lemma 1 (remainders can't be 2012) was really annoying; I got a faulty answer of 503 before realizing this. Essentially, without this discrepancy, we do not have $d_2$ , just $d_1$ , so we cannot remove that last pair. Also, phrasing Claim 2 exactly was quite annoying. I've tried to be very clear with my solution overall, since it's problem for which I needed to be extremely careful with all my assumptions.

The answer is $S = 502$ (not $503$ !).**Claim:** If $\gcd(k, 2012) = 1$ , then necessarily either $k$ or $2012-k$ will counts towards $S$ . *Proof.* First note that both $ak$ , $bk$ are nonzero modulo $2012$ . Note also that $ak \not\equiv bk \pmod{2012}$ . So if $r_a$ is the remainder of $ak \pmod{2012}$ , then $2012-r_a$ is the remainder of $a(2012-k) \pmod{2012}$ Similarly we can consider $r_b$ and $2012-r_b$ . As mentioned already, we have $r_a \neq r_b$ . So either $r_a > r_b$ or $2012-r_a > 2012-r_b$ . $\blacksquare$ This implies $S \ge \frac{1}{2} \varphi(2012) = 502$ . But this can actually be achieved by taking $a = 4$ and $b = 1010$ , since - If $k$ is even, then $ak \equiv bk \pmod{2012}$ so no even $k$ counts towards $S$ ; and - If $k \equiv 0 \pmod{503}$ , then $ak \equiv 0 \pmod{2012}$ so no such $k$ counts towards $S$ . This gives the final answer $S \ge 502$ .**Remark:** A similar proof works with $2012$ replaced by any $n$ and will give an answer of $\frac{1}{2}\varphi(n)$ . For composite $n$ , one uses the Chinese remainder theorem to pick distinct $a$ and $b$ not divisible by $n$ such that $\operatorname{lcm}(a-b, a) = n$ .

stem_md: A circle is divided into  $432$  congruent arcs by  $432$  points.  The points are colored in four colors such that some  $108$  points are colored Red, some  $108$  points are colored Green, some  $108$  points are colored Blue, and the remaining  $108$  points are colored Yellow.  Prove that one can choose three points of each color in such a way that the four triangles formed by the chosen points of the same color are congruent.

Let  $R, B, Y, G$  denote the set of all points that are red, blue, yellow, and green respectively. Denote the vertices as  $v_1, v_2, \dots, v_{12n}$ . We define the distance between two vertices  $v_i$  and  $v_j$  as  $|i - j|$ . Denote by  $N_R$  the set of all the differences from  $R$ . We then make the following observations: $\bullet$   $|N_R| \geq 3n - 1$ ; $\bullet$   $|N_R \cap N_B| \leq 3n - 1$ ; $\bullet$   $|N_R \cap N_B \cap N_Y| \geq n$ ; $\bullet$   $|N_R \cup N_B \cup N_Y \cup N_G| < 4n - 1 \implies |N_R \cup N_B \cup N_Y \cup N_G| \leq 4n - 2$ .

Also notice that if for three red vertices and three blue vertices  $(v_i, v_j, v_k)$  and  $(v_{i'}, v_{j'}, v_{k'})$  are such that  $d(v_i, v_k) = d(v_{i'}, v_{j'}), d(v_i, v_k) = d(v_{i'}, v_{k'})$ , then  $d(v_j, v_k) = d(v_{j'}, v_{k'})$ . Therefore it would suffice to show  $|N_R \cap N_B \cap N_Y \cap N_G| \geq 2$ . 

By inclusion-exclusion, we have that   $$ |N_R \cap N_B \cap N_Y \cap N_G| = |N_R| + |N_B| + |N_Y| + |N_G| - (|N_R \cap N_B| + |N_R \cap N_Y| + |N_R \cap N_G| + |N_B \cap N_Y| + |N_B \cap N_G| + |N_Y \cap N_G|) $$     $$ + (|N_R \cap N_B \cap N_Y| + |N_R \cap N_B \cap N_G| + |N_R \cap N_Y \cap N_G| + |N_B \cap N_Y \cap N_G|) - |N_R \cup N_B \cup N_Y \cup N_G| $$     $$ \geq 4(3n - 1) - 4(3n - 1) + 4n - (4n - 2) = 2,  $$   as desired.  $\blacksquare$

<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>**Lemma.** Designate  $k$  points which we shall call "good" on the 432-point circle. Then consider the 431 non-identity rotations of all the points of a given color. Then one of these rotations will hit at least  $\left\lceil\frac{108k}{431}\right\rceil$  good points.**Proof.** Let  $n_i$  be the number of good points that the  $i$ th rotation hits. The sum of all the  $n_i$  is just  $108k$  since each of the  $k$  good points are hit 108 times, so at least one of the  $n_i$  must be greater than or equal to the average, that is, there exists an  $n_i\geq\left\lceil\frac{108k}{431}\right\rceil$ .

So now designate the red points as the good points. One of the rotations of the green points will hit at least 28 good points, and call these the new good points. One of the rotations of the blue points will hit at least 8 good points, and call these the new good points. One of the rotations of the yellow points will hit at least 3 good points, and these points are the ones we want. If we un-rotate each of them to the original positions of each color, we get our four desired congruent triangles.</details>

Denote  $a_k$  to be the number of matches with the red points when you rotate the greens by  $k$ . Then  $a_1+\cdots+a_{431}=108^2$ . On average, each  $a$  is  $\frac{108^2}{431}>27$ , so at least rotation gives  $28$  matches. Then consider those  $28$  points. Let  $b_k$  be the number of matches with those with the blues when you rotate by  $k$ . Then  $b_1+\cdots+b_{431}=28*108$ . On average, each  $b$  is  $\frac{28\cdot 108}{431}>7$ , so at least one is  $8$ . Then, we do the same action again and get that we can rotate each of the colors to get a group of  $3$  that is the same, because  $\frac{108\cdot 8}{431}>2$ .

Claim: If there is a red  $n$  gon, then we can find a green  $\lceil \tfrac{108}{431} n \rceil$  gon such that there is some subset of the red polygon that is congruent to the green polygon.

Proof: Consider all 431 possible non-identity rotations; for each red point, the probability that it is mapped to a green point is  $\tfrac{108}{431}$ . Thus the expected value of the number of vertices of the  $n$  gon that are mapped to green points is  $\tfrac{108}{431} n$ . This means we can find some green  $\lceil \tfrac{108}{431} n \rceil$  gon as desired.

[rule]
By the claim, we can find a green  $\lceil \tfrac{108}{431} 108 \rceil = 28$  gon that is congruent to some subset of the red points. In addition, we can find a blue  $\lceil \tfrac{108}{431} 28 \rceil = 8$  gon that is congruent to some subset of the green  $28$  gon. Finally, we can find a yellow  $\lceil \tfrac{108}{431} 8 \rceil = 3$  gon that is congruent to some subset of the blue  $8$  gon, and we're done.

The key idea here is to notice that triangles on the circle are congruent if and only if they are rotations of one another. Thus, we can consider all possible rotations of the 108 points and see if at least 3 of them overlap with the other 3 colors. 


Let us deal with the blue points. Considering an arbitrary rotation, the probability a red point has been rotated onto a blue is  $\frac{1}{4}$ . Thus, the expected value of overlapping blue-red points is " on average"  $108 \cdot \frac{1}{4}=27$ . Now, take any rotation with at least 27 points. Rotating these points, we want to find the expected number of red-green overlaps. The expected value is  $27 \cdot \frac{1}{4}=\frac{27}{4}=6.75$ . Thus, there certainly \textit{exists} a rotation with at least 7 red-green overlaps. Take these 7 points. Then, we count the number of red-yellow overlaps. The expected number is  $\frac{7}{4}=1.75$ . However, this only guarantees there \textit{exists} 2 overlapping red-yellow points. However, we need 3! However, we can slightly improve this lower bound to 3 through a nice trick. Notice that there are on average 27 red-blue overlaps. However, the only way it is 27, and not anything lower or higher, ist that every single rotation has 27 overlapping red-blue points. However, we know that this is not true. For example, take the identity rotation for the red points. There are 0 red-blue overlaps. Therefore, there must be some rotation with over 27 overlapping points to "balance out" these lower values. Once again, using the same trick, since the identity rotation has 0 overlaps, there certainly exists a rotation with 3 red-yellow overlaps. Thus, we have found 4 triangles which are rotations of each other, as desired.

I think the solution follows super naturally from the ideas this problem embodies, which I'll state briefly below (and which I believe is more useful for my own storage anyways), so I'll leave out a full solution.

The idea is that *the bound is not tight enough*. Summing/expecting/pigeonholing/whatever in the obvious way yields a bound of  $\frac{108^4}{432^3-\varepsilon} < 2$  expected intersections between all four points. Upon inspection, however, this is a pretty loose bound: there are many cases where *things don't intersect* (i.e. the EV is 0) but they are counted in the numerator. Replacing  $432^3$  with  $431 \cdot 430 \cdot 429$  doesn't do much, either.

The piecemeal Pigeonhole application is simply to encode this emptiness as much as possible. Notice that at every step, the difference between 432 and 431 makes a critical difference: otherwise, we wouldn't have been able to construct the 28-gon (instead a 27-gon), 8-gon (instead a 7-gon), and so on; ignoring these slight non-identity irregularities turns this solution into essentially the global case (with only segments found), but taking advantage of the small alterations forms the crux of the solution.

I don't usually like writing explicit motivations, but I find this problem to be a perfect example of the importance of intermediate steps especially in global problems; the idea shines through without any other difficulty to cloud the problem.

The idea is to rotate the points of one color so that they overlap onto another color. Our goal is to rotate the colored points such that we can get three stacks of all four colors, which would imply that there is a congruent (in fact, rotationally congruent) triangle. 

First, fix  $108$  of the red points. We first rotate the blue points. Consider the  $108$  rotational states of the blue points. Then the expected value of the number of overlapping blue and red points is  $\frac{108}{4} = 27$  because there is a one fourth chance for a given point that it is blue. However, we know there is a state (the original) for which there are  $0$  overlapping points. This means there must exist  $28$  points that overlap for some rotation. 

Now we fix those  $28$  points and rotate the yellow points. The logic is the same, one fourth chance of overlapping, but a  $0$  state exists, so we have a rotation that has  $8$  points with red, blue, and yellow overlapping. Then, we can rotate green and we'll have  $\frac{8}{4} + 1 = 3$  points overlapping, resulting in a congruent triangle as desired.

This is a linearity of expectation problem, which was fairly obvious as there aren't any other obvious approaches. Trying smaller cases seems to suggest the the numbers hold some bearing, most likely to force the expectation to work.

Now rather than attempt to look at triangles, we instead consider rotating segments of a specific color. Indeed consider rotating all red arcs about the center of the circle, such that they map to some other arcs. Now if any  $3$  red arcs coincide with any  $3$  arcs of a different color, then connecting those arcs we find a congruent triangle shared by the two colors. Thus it suffices to show the expected value of arc overlaps shared amongst all colors is bounded between  $2$  and  $3$ .

Consider the expected number of arc overlaps for two specific colors, say red and blue. A specific red segment lies on any other blue segment with probability  $\frac{1}{431}$  over a random rotation. Thus the expected number of overlaps is  $108 \cdot \frac{108}{431} >108 \cdot \frac{1}{4} = 27$ . Thus for two specific colors we are guarenteed at least  $28$  overlaps.  A similar process allows us to find we are guarenteed an expected  $8$  arcs overlapping amongst  $3$  colors, and at least  $3$  overlapping arcs amongst  $4$ , as desired. **Remark:** The rotation idea also appears in a certain Canda problem in a walkthrough of D-Global.

Consider rotating these  $28$  points again in  $431$  ways, for an expected number of  $\lceil \frac{28 \cdot 108}{431} \rceil = 8$  points where red, green, and blue coincide. Repeating, we get  $\lceil \frac{8 \cdot 108}{431} \rceil > 2 $  so there exists three points. Because all we did is rotate, these three points after shifting back give us congruent triangles as required.

stem_md: Determine which integers  $n > 1$  have the property that there exists an infinite sequence  $a_1, a_2, a_3, \ldots$  of nonzero integers such that the equality \[a_k+2a_{2k}+\ldots+na_{nk}=0\]holds for every positive integer  $k$ .
solution_md:
The answer is $\boxed{n > 2}.$ First, notice that $n=2$ clearly doesn't work, as by induction $a_{1} = 2^{k}a_{2^{k}},$ absurd. [rule] The construction is the hard part. Claim: If there exists a sequence $a_{1}, \cdots, a_{n}$ such that $a_{ij} = a_{i}a_{j}$ for $ij \le n$ and $a_{1}+2a_{2}+\cdots+na_{n} = 0,$ then $n$ works.
ProofWe extend this $n$ term sequence to be infinitely long, by taking $a_{i}a_{j} = a_{ij}$ for all $i,j.$ Clearly, $a_{k}+\cdots+na_{nk} = a_{k}(a_{1}+\cdots+na_{n})=0,$ as desired. $\square$
We now need to find the $n$ where such a sequence exists. Notice that, for $m \ge 9,$ there is always a prime $p$ such that $m \le p < \frac{4}{3}m$ (a strengthened Bertrand's Postulate). So, in our case, we know that for $n \ge 18,$ there exists a prime in each of the intervals $\left[\frac{9}{16}n, \frac{3}{4}n\right)$ and $\left[\frac{3}{4}n, n\right),$ call them $p$ and $q,$ respectively. Choose $a_{p^{\prime}}$ to be anything for $p^{\prime} \neq p,q.$ Then, we can choose $a_{p},a_{q}$ so that $pa_{p}+qa_{q}= \ell,$ for some $\ell,$ since $\gcd(p,q)=1.$ Notice that this works as long as $\frac{n}{2} < p,q \le n.$ Since there are two primes between $\left(\frac{n}{2}, n\right]$ for $n = 5, 7, 8, 9, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17.$ So, it remains to verify $n = 3,4,6,10$ work. For $n = 3,$ take the sequence $(a_{1}, a_{2}, a_{3}) = (1,1,-1),$ for $n=4,$ take $(1,2,-7,4),$ for $n=6,$ take $(1,3,-4,9,-3,-12),$ and for $n=10,$ take $(1,2,1,4,3,2,8,8,1,6).$ . Thus, we have completed the problem.

<details><summary>Begin torture</summary>The answer is all  $n\geq 3$ . Of course,  $n=2$  doesn't work by infinite descent.

The algorithmic construction for  $n\geq 3$  is as follows:

For each  $k=1,2,3,\dots$  such that  $n\nmid k$ , do the following:
(a) For  $m=1,2,\dots,n-2$ , if  $a_{km}$  is already defined, do nothing, otherwise set  $a_{km}=1$  (this is arbitrary).
(b) Then put in  $a_{k(n-1)}$  an integer such that  $a_{k(n-1)}\equiv a_k+2a_{2k}+\dots+(n-2)a_{(n-2)k}\pmod n$ . In this way, we can put
(c)  $a_{kn}=\frac{-a_k-2a_{2k}-\dots-(n-1)a_{(n-1)k}}{n}$ , and by (b), this is an integer and  $a_k+2a_{2k}+\dots+na_{nk}=0$ .
Also call part (c) of this operation a  $k$ -run.

Now for each  $p=1,2,3,\dots$ , we still need to modify the sequence so that  $a_{n^pk}+2a_{2n^pk}+\dots+(n-1)a_{(n-1)n^pk}$  is divisible by  $n$  for each  $k$  with  $n\nmid k$ . We can do this as follows:

For  $p=1,2,3,\dots$ , and for each  $k=1,2,3,\dots$  such that  $n\nmid k$ , let  $x_{k,p}$  be the remainder when  $a_{n^pk}+2a_{2n^pk}+\dots+(n-1)a_{(n-1)n^pk}$  is divided by  $n$ . Then do the following:
- Add  $n^px_{k,p}$  to  $a_{(n-1)^{p+1}k}$ .
- Perform a  $(n-1)^{p+1}k$ -run. This will add  $n^{p-1}x_{k,p}$  to  $a_{(n-1)^pnk}$  (modulo  $n^p$ ).
- Perform a  $(n-1)^pnk$ -run. This will add  $n^{p-2}x_{k,p}$  to  $a_{(n-1)^{p-1}n^2k}$ .
... and so on, ... until
- Perform a  $(n-1)^2n^{p-1}k$ -run. This will add  $x_{k,p}$  to  $a_{(n-1)n^pk}$ .
- We can now put an integer for  $a_{n^{p+1}k}$ .
Now changing some of the numbers may change other numbers, but these other numbers are separate from this process and we will only need to correct for this by changing the last number in any such modified sequence. So although this is an infinite process, we are guaranteed that for each  $\ell$ , at some finite point,  $a_\ell$  stops changing. So this infinite sequence exists.

<details><summary>My solution</summary>First let's state Bertrand's postulate: For any real  $x>1$ , there is a prime in the half-open interval  $[x, 2x)$ .

Let's do some easy cases first.  $n=2$  is impossible, of course.  If  $n=4$ : Let  $i=2^k3^lm$  where  $m$  is divisible by neither  $2$  nor  $3$ .  Then  $a_i=2^k(-7)^l$  works:  $a_i+2a_{2i}+3a_{3i}+4a_{4i}=a_i(1+2\cdot2+3\cdot(-7)+4\cdot4)=0$ .

So otherwise we assume  $n\neq4$  and  $n>2$ .  We find two distinct primes  $p_1$  and  $p_2$  so that  $\sqrt{n}<p_1\leq n$  and  $\frac{n}{2}<p_2<n$ .  For  $n=3$  we can choose  $p_1=3$  and  $p_2=2$ .  For  $n=5$  we can choose  $p_1=5$  and  $p_2=3$ ; for  $n=6$  through  $n=8$  we can choose  $p_1=3$  and  $p_2=5$ ; from  $n=9$  through  $n=13$  we can choose  $p_1=5$  and  $p_2=7$ , and from  $n=14$  to  $n=24$  we can choose  $p_1=5$  and  $p_2=13$ .

Beyond this, if  $n$  is even, then take  $x=\frac{n+1}{2}$  in Bertrand's postulate.  This shows that there is a prime in the interval  $\left[\frac{n+1}{2}, n+1\right)$  or (equivalently) the interval  $\left[\frac{n+1}{2}, n\right]$ .  But  $n$  is even so it can't be prime.  Thus there is a prime in the interval  $\left[\frac{n+1}{2}, n-1\right]$ , call it  $p_2$  because  $\frac{n}{2}<\frac{n+1}{2}\leq p_2\leq n-1<n$ .  If  $n$  is odd, we choose instead  $x=\frac{n}{2}$ .  There is thus a prime in the interval  $\left[\frac{n}{2}, n\right)$ .  But  $\frac{n}{2}$  is not an integer, so we shrink the interval to  $\left[\frac{n+1}{2}, n-1\right]$ .  Then let this prime be  $p_2$ ; it works for the same reasons.

Then there is a prime again in the interval  $\left[\frac{p_2}{2}, p_2\right)$ , call it  $p_1$ .  But  $p_1\geq\frac{p_2}{2}>\frac{n}{4}>\frac{\sqrt{n}\sqrt{16}}{4}=\sqrt{n}$ .  And clearly  $p_1<p_2<n$ .

So now, for all  $n\neq4$  we've found two primes  $p_1$  and  $p_2$  with  $\frac{n}{2}<p_2<n$  and  $\sqrt{n}<p_1\leq n$ .  So now for every other prime besides  $p_1$  and  $p_2$ , we define  $a_{p_k}=p_2$ .  But there is some  $x, y$  (by Bezout's theorem) so that  $1+xp_1=yp_2$ ; let  $a_{p_1}=x$ .  Then for all  $m$  not divisible by  $p_2$ , if  $m=p_1^{e_1}p_3^{e_3}p_4^{e_4}\ldots$  then let  $a_m=a_{p_1}^{e_1}a_{p_3}^{e_3}a_{p_4}^{e_4}\ldots$ ; in other words, make it totally multiplicative.  Finally let  $a_1=1$ .

Then all numbers less than or equal to  $n$  that are not  $1$ ,  $p_1$  or  $p_2$  have a prime factor that is not  $p_1$  or  $p_2$  (because  $p_1$  and  $p_2$  are greater than  $\sqrt{n}$ ), and so all numbers  $i$  that are not  $p_1$  or  $p_2$  have  $p_2|a_i$ .

So then the number  $\frac{-a_1-2a_2-3a_3-\ldots-(p_2-1)a_{p_2-1}-(p_2+1)a_{p_2+1}-\ldots-na_n}{p_2}$  is just  $\frac{-1-p_1a_{p_1}}{p_2}-m=\frac{-1-xp_1}{p_2}-m=-y-m$  for some integer  $m$ .  We let  $-y-m$  be  $a_{p_2}$ , so that  $a_1+2a_2+\ldots+na_n=0$ .

Thus  $a_k+2a_{2k}+3a_{3k}+\ldots+na_{nk}=a_k(a_1+2a_2+3a_3+\ldots+na_n)=0$  because we made it totally multiplicative, so we can pull the factor of  $a_k$  out whatever  $k$  may be.  Thus we're done.</details>

For  $n = 2$ , we have  $a_k + 2a_{2k} = 0$ , which is clearly not possible, since it implies  $a_{2^k} = \frac{a_1}{2^k}$  for all  $k$ .

For  $n \ge 3$  we will construct a *completely multiplicative* sequence (meaning  $a_{ij} = a_i a_j$  for all  $i$  and  $j$ ). Thus  $(a_i)$  is determined by its value on primes, and satisfies the condition as long as  $a_1 + 2a_2 + \dots + na_n = 0$ . The idea is to take two large primes and use Bezout's theorem, but the details require significant care.

We start by solving the case where  $n \ge 9$ . In that case, by Bertrand postulate there exists primes  $p$  and  $q$  such that \[ 	\left\lceil n/2 \right\rceil < q < 2\left\lceil n/2 \right\rceil. 	\quad\text{and}\quad 	\frac{1}{2}(q-1) < p < q-1 \] Clearly  $p \neq q$ , and  $q \ge 7$ , so  $p > 3$ . Also,  $p < q < n$  but  $2q > n$ , and  $4p \ge 4\left( \frac{1}{2}(q+1) \right) > n$ . We now stipulate that  $a_r = 1$  for any prime  $r \neq p,q$  (in particular including  $r=2$  and  $r=3$ ). There are now three cases, identical in substance.  	
- If  $p, 2p, 3p \in [1,n]$  then we would like to 	choose nonzero  $a_p$  and  $a_q$  such that 	\[ 6p \cdot a_p + q \cdot a_q = 6p + q - \frac{1}{2} n (n+1) \] 	which is possible by B\'ezout lemma, since  $\gcd(6p,q) = 1$ .
- Else if  $p, 2p \in [1,n]$  then we would like to 	choose nonzero  $a_p$  and  $a_q$  such that 	\[ 3p \cdot a_p + q \cdot a_q = 3p + q - \frac{1}{2} n (n+1) \] 	which is possible by B\'ezout lemma, since  $\gcd(3p, q) = 1$ .
- Else if  $p \in [1,n]$  then we would like to 	choose nonzero  $a_p$  and  $a_q$  such that 	\[ p \cdot a_p + q \cdot a_q = p + q - \frac{1}{2} n (n+1) \] 	which is possible by B\'ezout lemma, since  $\gcd(p, q) = 1$ . 	(This case is actually possible in a few edge cases, 	for example when  $n=9$ ,  $q=7$ ,  $p=5$ .) [/list]

It remains to resolve the cases where  $3 \le n \le 8$ . We enumerate these cases manually: [list]
- For  $n = 3$ , let  $a_n = (-1)^{\nu_3(n)}$ .
- For  $n = 4$ , let  $a_n = (-1)^{\nu_2(n) + \nu_3(n)}$ .
- For  $n = 5$ , let  $a_n = (-2)^{\nu_5(n)}$ .

Now we show all  $n > 2$  work. **Claim:** For all  $n \geq 3,$  let  $p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_r$  be the set of primes less than or equal to  $n,$  in increasing order. Then we can choose nonzero integers  $c_1, c_2, \ldots, c_r$  such that   $$ \sum_{m = 1}^n m \cdot \left(\prod_{i = 1}^r c_i^{v_{p_i}(m)}\right) = 0. $$  *Proof:* First we show this is true for all  $n \geq 16.$ By Bertrand's Postulate (which states that for all  $n > 1,$  there is a prime  $p$  with  $n < p < 2n$ ), there is a prime in the interval  $\left(\lceil{\frac{n}{4}}\rceil, 2\lceil{\frac{n}{4}}\rceil\right)$ , and a prime in the interval  $\left(\lceil{\frac{n}{2}}\rceil, 2\lceil{\frac{n}{2}}\rceil\right)$ . Also, there is no integer in both intervals - this would require  $2\lceil{\frac{n}{4}}\rceil \geq \lceil{\frac{n}{2}}\rceil + 2$  (because the integer  $k$  would need to satisfy  $k \geq 2\lceil{\frac{n}{4}}\rceil + 1$  and  $k \leq \lceil{\frac{n}{2}}\rceil - 1$ ), and this never happens (we can check this is false for  $n = 0, 1, 2, 3,$  so by writing  $n = 4a + b$  with  $b \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\},$  it is false for all  $n$ ). This means the two primes are distinct. So then  $p_r > \frac{n}{2}$  and  $p_{r - 1} > \frac{n}{4}.$ Now set  $c_i = 1$  for  $1 \leq i \leq r - 2,$  and let  $S$  be the sum over all  $m$  not divisible by  $p_r$  or  $p_{r - 1}$  (of the given quantity). Since  $n \geq 16,$  then  $p_{r - 1}^2, p_{r - 1}p_r,$  and  $p_r^2$  are greater than  $n,$  so each  $m$  is divisible by at most one of them, and is never divisible by their squares (for  $1 \leq m \leq n$ ). Since  $2p_r > n,$  the only term containing  $p_r$  is  $m = p_r,$  which contributes  $p_r \cdot c_r$  to the sum. Since  $4p_{r - 1} > n,$  the set of terms containing  $p_{r - 1}$  is one of  $\{p_{r - 1}\}, \{p_{r - 1}, 2p_{r - 1}\},$  or  $\{p_{r - 1}, 2p_{r - 1}, 3p_{r - 1}\},$  so its contribution to the sum is  $p_{r - 1}\cdot c_{r - 1}\cdot k,$  where  $k \in \{1, 3, 6\}.$  So then the entire sum is   $$ S + c_r\cdot p_r + c_{r - 1}\cdot kp_{r - 1}, $$   where  $k \in \{1, 3, 6\},$  and we need to choose  $c_r, c_{r - 1}$  so that this sum is  $0.$  But  $p_r$  and  $kp_{r - 1}$  are relatively prime (because  $p_r \neq 2, 3$ ), so we can choose  $c_r$  and  $c_{r - 1}$  which make  $c_r\cdot p_r + c_{r - 1}\cdot kp_{r - 1}$  to be any integer, which means we can make it  $-S.$  Also, if  $(c_r, c_{r - 1})$  works, then  $(c_r - kp_{r - 1}, c_{r - 1} + p_r)$  also works, so we can repeatedly do this until  $c_r$  is negative and  $c_{r - 1}$  is positive. Then neither is  $0,$  so we are done.

Now we show this is true for  $3 \leq n \leq 15.$ For  $n = 3,$  we can choose  $c_1 = 1$  (corresponding to  $p_1 = 2$ ) and  $c_2 = -1$  (corresponding to  $p_2 = 3$ ), as  $1\cdot 1 + 2\cdot 1 + 3 \cdot (-1) = 0.$ For  $n = 4,$  we can choose  $c_1 = c_2 = -1$  (corresponding to  $p_1 = 2, p_2 = 3$ ), as  $1 \cdot 1 + 2\cdot (-1) + 3\cdot (-1) + 4\cdot 1 = 0.$ For  $n = 5,$  we can choose  $c_1 = c_2 = 1$  (corresponding to  $p_1 = 2, p_2 = 3$ ) and  $c_3 = -2$  (corresponding to  $p_3 = 5$ ), as  $1\cdot 1 + 2\cdot 1 + 3\cdot 1 + 4\cdot 1 + 5\cdot (-2) = 0.$ For  $n = 6,$  we can choose  $c_1 = 1$  (for  $p_1 = 2$ ),  $c_2 = 2$  (for  $p_2 = 3$ ), and  $c_3 = -5$  (for  $p_3 = 5$ ), as  $1\cdot 1 + 2\cdot 1 + 3\cdot 2 + 4\cdot 1 + 5\cdot (-5) + 6\cdot 2 = 0.$ For  $7 \leq n \leq 15,$  we can check that  $p_r > p_{r - 1} \geq \frac{n}{2}.$  Then the same argument applies - we can let  $c_i = 1$  for  $1 \leq i \leq r - 2,$  and let  $S$  be the sum of the given expression over all  $m$  not divisible by  $p_{r - 1}$  or  $p_r.$  Then since  $n > 4,$  all of  $p_{r - 1}^2, p_{r-1}p_r,$  and  $p_r^2$  are greater than  $n.$  Then the sum is   $$ S + c_r\cdot p_r + c_{r - 1}\cdot kp_{r - 1}, $$   where  $k \in \{1, 3\}.$  Since  $p_r \neq 3,$  then  $p_r$  and  $kp_{r - 1}$  are relatively prime, so by the same reasoning as before, it is possible to choose nonzero  $c_r, c_{r - 1}$  so that this sum is  $0.$  

So then it is possible to choose such  $c_i$  for all  $n \geq 3.$ Now we show that taking  $a_k = \prod_{i = 1}^r c_i^{v_{p_i}(k)}$  for all positive integers  $k$  satisfies the problem. We have  $v_p(mn) = v_p(m) + v_p(n),$  so then 
\begin{align*}
    \sum_{m = 1}^n ma_{mk} &= \sum_{m = 1}^n m\prod_{i = 1}^r c_i^{v_{p_i}(mk)} 
    &= \prod_{i = 1}^r c_i^{v_{p_i}(k)} \cdot \left(\sum_{m = 1}^n m\prod_{i = 1}^r c_i^{v_{p_i}(m)} \right) 
    &= 0,
\end{align*}
by our choice of the  $c_i.$  So then there exist such  $a_i$  for all  $n > 2.$</details>

We claim that $n$ works iff $n\ge 2$ . First, we show that $n=2$ does not satisfy this property. For the base case, remark that $a_1=-2a_2$ because $a_1+2a_2=0$ . <details><summary>Solution</summary>Note that  $f(1!) = f(1)! \rightarrow f(1) = f(1)!$ , which only happens when  $f(1)$  is equal  $1$  or  $2$ . Additionally,  $f(2!) = f(2)! \rightarrow f(2) = f(2)!$ , which again only happens when  $f(2)$  equals  $1$  or  $2$ . We then break this problem into cases.

<u>Case 1:</u>  $f(1) = 2, f(2) = 1$ .
Since we must have that  $m - n$  must divide  $f(m) - f(n)$  for all distinct integers  $m, n$ , we must have that  $(3! - 1) \mid (f(3)! - 2)$  as well as  $(3! - 2) \mid (f(3)! - 1)$ . But if  $f(3) = 1$ , then  $(3! - 1) \nmid (f(3)! - 2)$ , and if  $f(3) = 2$ , then  $(3! - 2) \nmid (f(3)! - 1)$ . Moreover, if  $f(3)$  is a positive integer greater than  $2$ , then  $f(3)! - 1$  will always be odd while  $3! - 2$  will always be even. Let  $k$  be a positive integer. If  $k > 2$ ,  $(3! - 2) \nmid (f(3)! - 1)$ . So we have no possible functions for this case.

<u>Case 2:</u>  $f(1) = f(2) = 1$ .
Here, we claim that  $f(k) = 1$  for all positive integers  $k$ . We can easily check that  $f(k) = 1$  works since  $f(x!) = f(x)! = 1$  for all  $x$ , and  $(m - n) \mid (1 - 1)$  for all distinct positive integers  $m, n$ . Suppose for the sake of contradiction that  $f(k)$  does not equal  $1$  for all  $k$ . We must have that  $(k! - 2) \mid (f(k)! - 1)$  for all  $k > 2$  if we let  $m = k!$  and  $n = 2$ . But notice that  $f(k)! - 1$  will always be odd if  $f(k)$  is at least  $2$  while  $k! - 2$  is always even for  $k > 2$ . So  $(k! - 2) \nmid (f(k)! - 1)$  for  $f(k) \ne 1$ , contradiction. Hence,  $f(k)$  must equal  $1$  for all  $k$ , so  $f(x) = 1$  is a possible solution.

<u>Case 3:</u>  $f(1) = f(2) = 2$ .
Now, we claim that  $f(k) = 2$  for all positive integers  $k$ . Again, we can easily check that  $f(k) = 2$  satisfies that problem's conditions for all  $k$ . To prove that  $f(k)$  must equal  $2$ , we can use a slick induction. We have that our base case is  $f(1) = f(2) = f(3) = 2$  since  $f(3) = 2$  is the only value for  $f(3)$  that satisfies  $(3! - 1) \mid (f(3)! - 2)$  and  $(3! - 2) \mid (f(3)! - 2)$ . Now suppose that  $f(k) = 2$  for all positive integers up to  $k$ . We wish to show that  $f(k + 1) = 2$ . Then,  $f((k + 1)!)$  must satisfy   $$ ((k + 1)! - 1) \mid (f(k + 1)! - 2), ((k + 1)! - 2) \mid (f(k + 1)! - 2), \ldots , ((k + 1)! - k) \mid (f(k + 1)! - 2). $$   So if  $((k + 1)! - 1) \mid (f(k + 1)! - 2)$ , then  $(k + 1)! - 1 = b_0$ , and  $f(k + 1)! - 2 = c_0b_0$ , where  $b_0$  is an integer and  $c_0$  is a polynomial in terms of  $b_0$ . Now let  $P(b_0) = f(k + 1)! - 2 = c_0b_0$ . Then, we must have that  $b_0 - 1, b_0 - 2, \ldots , b_0 - k + 1$  divides  $P(b_0)$ . But in order for this to happen,  $P(b_0)$  must have a root at  $b_0 = 1, 2, \ldots , k - 1$ , by the Factor Theorem. Thus, we have  $P(k - 1) = 0 = f(k + 1)! - 2$ , which rearranges into  $f(k + 1)! = 2$ . The only solution to this is  $f(k + 1) = 2$ , so our induction is complete. We have that  $f(x) = 2$  is another possible solution.

<u>Case 4:</u>  $f(1) = 1, f(2) = 2$ .
For our fourth and final case, perform a similar induction as in case 3. Here, we claim that  $f(k) = k$  for all  $k$ . We have that our base case is  $f(1) = 1$ ,  $f(2) = 2$ , and  $f(3) = 3$  since  $f(3) = 3$  is the only integer satisfying  $(3! - 1) \mid (f(3)! - 1)$  and  $(3! - 2) \mid (f(3)! - 2)$ . Now assume  $f(k) = k$  for all positive integers up to  $k$ . We aim to prove that  $f(k + 1) = k + 1$ . Here, we need   $$ ((k + 1)! - 1) \mid (f(k + 1)! - 1), ((k + 1)! - 2) \mid (f(k + 1)! - 2), \ldots , ((k + 1)! - k) \mid (f(k + 1)! - k). $$   If  $(k + 1)! - 1$  divides  $f(k + 1)! - 1$ , then we have that  $(k + 1)! - 1 = b_1$  and  $f(k + 1)! - 1 = c_1b_1$ , with  $c_1$  and  $b_1$  defined in the same way as  $c_0$  and  $b_0$ , respectively. Set  $P(b_1) = c_1b_1$ . In order for  $b_1 - 1, b_1 - 2, \ldots , b_1 - k + 1$  to divide  $P(b_1)$ , we need  $P(1) = 1, P(2) = 2, \ldots , P(k - 1) = k - 1$ . Since  $((k + 1)! - (k + 1)) \mid (f(k + 1)! - f(k + 1))$  must also be true, and  $(k + 1)! - (k + 1) = b_1 - k$ , we need   $$ f(k + 1)! - 1 - f(k + 1) + 1 = c_1b_1 - f(k + 1) + 1 = 0 $$   when  $b_1 = k$ . But  $P(k - 1) = c_1(k - 1) = k - 1$  implies that  $c_1 = 1$ , so we have  $k - f(k + 1) + 1 = 0 \rightarrow f(k + 1) = k + 1$  after plugging in  $1$  for  $c_1$  and  $k$  for  $b_1$ . Our induction is finally complete, so  $f(x) = x$  is the final solution.

Thus, all possible functions are  $\boxed{f(x) = 1, f(x) = 2,}$  and  $\boxed{f(x) = x.}$</details>

Case 1:  $f(1)=f(2)=1.$  Then for all  $n,$  we have  $f(n) \equiv 1 \pmod{n-1}$  and  $f(n) \equiv 1 \pmod{n-2}$ , so  $f(n) \equiv 1 \pmod{(n-1)(n-2)}.$  But then  $f(n)! \equiv 1 \pmod{(n!-1)(n!-2)}$  so  $f(n)=1$  for all  $n$  since  $f(n)!$  has to be odd.

Case 2:  $f(1)=f(2)=2.$  We claim  $f(3)=2$ . With a similar argument as above, we have  $f(3) \equiv 0 \pmod 2$  and  $f(6) \equiv 2 \pmod {20},$  so  $4\nmid f(3)!$  which means  $f(3)<4$  or  $f(3)=2.$  Then for  $n>3$ , we have  $f(n)! \equiv 2 \pmod{\text{lcm}(n!-1, n!-2, n!-3)}$ , so  $3\nmid f(n)!$  which means  $f(n) <3$ . But since  $f(n)$  is even,  $f(n)=2$  as desired.

Case 3:  $f(1)=2,f(1)=2$ . We find that  $f(3) \equiv 0 \pmod 2$  and  $f(6) \equiv 17 \pmod{20}$ , but this is obviously impossible.

Case 4:  $f(1)=1, f(2)=2$ . We prove by induction  $f(n)=n$  for all  $n$ . The base case is  $n=3$ . We have  $f(3) \equiv 1 \pmod 2$  and  $f(3)!= f(6) \equiv 6 \pmod{20},$  so  $f(3) <4$  and  $f(3)=3$ . Assume that  $f(n)=n$  for  $n\leq k$ . Then we see that  $f(k+1) \equiv i \pmod{k+1-i}$  for all  $1\leq i \leq k$ , so  $f(k+1) \equiv k+1 \pmod{i}$  for all  $1\leq i \leq k$ . We can simplify this to  $f(k+1) \equiv k+1 \pmod{\text{lcm}(1,2,\dots, k)}$ . We also have  $f(k+1)! \equiv (k+1)! \pmod{\text{lcm}(1,2,\dots, (k+1)!-1)}$ . It is trivial to see that  $\text{lcm}(1,2,\dots, k) \geq k+1$ , so by Bertrand's postulate, there exists a prime  $p$  such that  $k+1 < p < k+1 + \text{lcm}(1,2,\dots, k) < (k+1)!$ . This means  $f(k+1)=k+1$ , or else, we would have an unwanted prime factor in  $f(k+1)!$  which would contradict the modulo statement ( $p$  would divide  $f(k+1)!$  and it divides the stuff inside the modulo,  $\text{lcm}(1,2,\dots,(k+1)!-1)$ , so it must divide  $(k+1)!$  and it doesn't.)

and  $a_0 < a_1 < \cdots$  which is enough.  $\square$ Now note that  $f(1) = f(1)!$  so  $f(1) \in \{1, 2 \}$ . We consider cases. $\textbf{Case 1:}$   $f(1) = 2$ First note that  $n = 3$  in the first equation gives  $f(6) = f(3)!$ . Now  $6 - 1 \mid f(6) - f(1) \implies f(3)! \equiv 2 \pmod{5}$ . Thus, it suffices to check  $f(3) = 1, 2, 3, 4,$  to which by inspection only  $f(3) = 2$  can hold. . $\textbf{Claim:}$   $f(n) \equiv 2$  for all  $n \in \mathbb{Z}^+$ Since  $f(3) = 2$ , Lemma 1 tells us that an infinite number of  $k$  satisfy  $f(k) = 2$ . For each  $k$ , we have  $n - k \mid f(n) - f(k) = f(n) - 2$ . But this implies  $f(n) - 2$  has an infinite number of integer divisors, so it must equal  $0$ . So  $f(n) = 2$  for each  $n$  as needed.  $\square$ So this case yields  $f(n) \equiv 2$  as a solution.  $\square$  $\textbf{Case 2:}$   $f(1) = 1$ Again, we have  $f(6) = f(3)!$ , and  $6 - 1 \mid f(6) - f(1) \implies f(3)! \equiv 1 \pmod{5}$ . Inspection on  $f(3) = 1, 2, 3, 4,$  implies only  $f(3) = 1$  or  $f(3) = 3$  can hold. $\textbf{Subcase 2.1:}$   $f(3) = 1$ .
Applying Lemma 1, an infinite number of  $k$  satisfy  $f(k) = 1$ , so for any  $k$  satisfying this and each  $n$  we have  $n - k \mid f(n) - f(k) = f(n) - 1$ . Since an infinite number of  $k$  work,  $f(n) - 1 = 0 \implies f(n) = 1$ . This argument holds for any  $n$  so  $f(n) \equiv 1$  is the only solution from this case.  $\square$  $\textbf{Subcase 2.2:}$   $f(3) = 3$ .
Note that if  $f(m) = m$ , we have  $f(m!) = m!$  and for  $m \ge 3$  we know that  $m < m!$ . Thus if we define  $b_i$  as the factorial applied onto  $3$  a total of  $i$  times we have  $f(b_0) = f(b_1) = \cdots$  implying an infinite number of  $k$  satisfy  $f(k) = k$ . 

Now consider any  $n$  and assert a  $k$  satisfying the latter, we have 
\[ n - k \mid f(n) - f(k) = f(n) - k \implies n - k \mid f(n) - n \]
so  $f(n) - n$  has an infinite number of integer divisors, implying it vanishes and thus  $f(n) = n$ . So this case yields  $f(n) \equiv n$  as a solution.  $\square$ All in all, we have exhausted all cases of the problem and have obtained the claimed solution set.  $\blacksquare$

For integer  $n\geq2$ , let  $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$  be real numbers satisfying \[x_1+x_2+\ldots+x_n=0, \qquad \text{and}\qquad x_1^2+x_2^2+\ldots+x_n^2=1.\]For each subset  $A\subseteq\{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$ , define\[S_A=\sum_{i\in A}x_i.\](If  $A$  is the empty set, then  $S_A=0$ .)

Prove that for any positive number  $\lambda$ , the number of sets  $A$  satisfying  $S_A\geq\lambda$  is at most  $2^{n-3}/\lambda^2$ .  For which choices of  $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n, \lambda$  does equality hold?
solution_md:
Solved with **GoodMorning**. 

Claim:  $\sum_{A\subseteq \{1,2,\ldots, n\} }S_A^2  = 2^{n-2}$  
Proof: We have \begin{align*}
\sum_{A\subseteq \{1,2,\ldots, n\} }S_A^2 = \sum_{A\subseteq \{1,2,\ldots, n\} } \sum_{i < j \in A} 2x_i x_j + \sum_{A\subseteq \{1,2,\ldots, n\}} \sum_{i\in A } x_i^2  
= 2^{n-1} ( \sum_{1\le i<j\le n } x_i x_j + \sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 )
2^{n-2} 
\end{align*} because  $\sum_{1\le i < j \le n}x_i x_j  = \frac{0^2 - 1}{2} = -\frac{1}{2} $ .  $\square$ Suppose FTSOC we had more than  $\frac{2^{n-3}}{\lambda^2}$  sets  $A$  with  $S_A \ge \lambda$ . Then the sum of  $S_A^2 $  over all these sets is more than  $\frac{2^{n-3}}{\lambda^2} \cdot \lambda^2 = 2^{n-3} $ . But notice that  $S_A^2$  equals  $S_B^2$ , where  $B$  is the complement of  $A$  (we have  $S_A = - S_B$ ). This implies that \[ \sum S_A^2 = 2\sum_{S_A > 0} S_A^2 > 2 \cdot 2^{n-3} = 2^{n-2}, \] contradiction. 

Now suppose equality held. Since  $\sum S_A^2 \ge 2\sum_{S_A > 0} S_A^2,$  we must have  $\sum_{S_A>0}S_A^2 \le 2^{n-3}$ . 

Notice that  $\sum_{S_A \ge \lambda} S_A^2$  is at least  $\frac{2^{n-3}}{\lambda^2}  \cdot \lambda^2 = 2^{n-3}$ . However, we also have  $\sum_{S_A \ge \lambda} S_A^2 \le \sum_{S_A > 0} S_A^2\le 2^{n-3}$ . This implies that  $\sum_{S_A \ge \lambda} S_A^2  = \sum_{S_A > 0 } S_A^2  = 2^{n-3}$ . Therefore, there are no sets  $A$  with  $0<S_A < \lambda$ . If there was some set  $A$  with  $S_A > \lambda$ , then we would have  $\sum_{S_A \ge \lambda} S_A^2 >  2^{n-3}$ , absurd. Thus, the only nonnegative possible values of  $S_A$  are  $0$  and  $\lambda$ . By taking the complement of  $A$ , the only negative value for  $S_A$  is  $-\lambda$ . 

This implies that all  $x_i$  are equal to  $0, \lambda, $  or  $-\lambda$ . Notice there must be the same number of  $\lambda$ s as  $-\lambda$ s. If there were two or more of each of these, then there exists an  $A$  with  $S_A = 2\lambda$ , but this means  $2\lambda \in \{0,\lambda, -\lambda\}$ , so  $\lambda = 0$ , absurd. Clearly we cannot have all  $x_i$  equal zero. Therefore  $(x_i)$  consists of one  $\lambda$ , one  $-\lambda$ , and  $n-2$  zeroes. So  $2\lambda^2 = 1\implies \lambda = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$ . So the only equality cases are \[ \boxed{ \left( -\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}, \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}, 0, 0, \ldots, 0  \right)}\] and permutations, which clearly work (with  $\lambda = -\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$ ).

<details><summary>Proof</summary>Let  $P$  be the power set of  $\{1,2,\dots,n\},$  with  $|P|=2^n.$  Let  $\mathbf{1}_A(i)=1$  if  $i\in A$  and equal zero if  $i\notin A.$  Now all sums on  $i$  or  $j$  are going to be over the whole set  $\{1,\dots,n\}$ With that notation,  $S(A)=\sum_i\mathbf{1}_A(i)x_i.$ Now, because this is the  $L^2$  version of Chebyshev, we need the "integral" of the square of  $S(A).$ \begin{align*}\sum_{A\in P}S(A)^2&=\sum_{A\in P}\left(\sum_i\mathbf{1}_A(i)x_i\right)\left(\sum_j\mathbf{1}_A(j)x_j\right)
&=\sum_i\sum_j\left(\sum_{A\in P}\mathbf{1}_A(i)\mathbf{1}_A(j)\right)x_ix_j\end{align*}
Now,  $\sum_{A\in P}\mathbf{1}_A(i)\mathbf{1}_A(j)$  counts how many sets there are that contain both  $i$  and  $j.$  There are two cases. If  $i=j,$  there are  $2^{n-1}$  such sets  $A,$  and if  $i\ne j,$  there are  $2^{n-2}$  such sets. So, continuing:
\begin{align*}\sum_{A\in P}S(A)^2&=2^{n-2}\left(2\sum_ix_i^2+\sum_{i\ne j}x_ix_j\right)
&=2^{n-2}\left(\sum_ix_i^2+\sum_i\sum_jx_ix_j\right)
&=2^{n-2}\left(\sum_ix_i^2+\left(\sum_ix_i\right)^2\right)
&=2^{n-2}(1+0)=2^{n-2}\end{align*}
Now define  $B_\lambda=\{A\in P\mid S(A)\ge \lambda\}$  and also define  $B_\lambda^*=\{A\in P\mid S(A)\le -\lambda\}.$  We claim that since the  $x_i$  sum to zero, then  $A$  is in  $B_\lambda$  if and only if the complement of  $A$  is in  $B_\lambda^*.$  That means that  $B_\lambda$  and  $B_\lambda^*$  are disjoint and  $|B_\lambda^*|=|B_\lambda|.$ Now we offer the standard proof of Chebyshev's Inequality. Let  $g(A)=\lambda^2$  for  $A\in B_\lambda\cup B_\lambda^*$  and zero otherwise. Note that  $g(A)\le S(A)^2$  for every  $A.$  Hence
\[\lambda^2|B_\lambda\cup B_\lambda^*|=\sum_{A\in P}g(A)\le\sum_{A\in P}S(A)^2=2^{n-2}\]
It now follows immediately that  $|B_\lambda|\le\frac{2^{n-3}}{\lambda^2}.$ As for the criterion for equality: that would require that  $g(A)=S(A)^2$  for every  $A$  in that last proof. Which would mean that  $S(A)=\lambda$  exactly for each  $A\in B_\lambda$  and zero for  $A$  in neither  $B_\lambda$  or  $B_\lambda^*.$  Pursuing the consequences of that, we wind up with the list of the  $x_i$  needing to be  $(\lambda, -\lambda, 0, 0,\dots,0)$  or some permutation of that. And with the sum of the squares being  $1,$  we get that  $\lambda=\frac1{\sqrt{2}}.$</details>

If x is a random variable, define E[x] to be the expected value of x. The Variance of x, which we will denote Var[x], is E[(x-E[x])^2].

A special case of what is called "The Second Moment Method" in combinatorics is the following theorem:

If x1, x2,..., xn are independent random variables, then 

Var[x1+x2+....+xn] = Var[x1]+Var[x2]+...+Var[xn].

So using the construction in our previous post, the conditions are equivalent to (if we set x = the random variable corresponding to the sum of xi)

E[x] = 0.
Var[x] = 1.

Or, rewriting with the definition of variance,

E[x] = 0.
E[x^2] = 1.

*Lemma: (Chebyshev)* For any positive  $\epsilon$  and random variable  $X$ ,
\[\text{Pr}\left(|X-\mu| \ge \epsilon \sigma\right) \le \frac{1}{\epsilon^2}\]
where  $\mu$  is the expected value of  $X$  and  $\sigma^2$  is its variance.

*Proof:*
\[\sigma^2 = \mathbb{E}((X-\mu)^2) \ge \epsilon^2 \sigma^2 \text{Pr}\left(|X-\mu| \ge \epsilon \sigma\right)\]
from which the result follows.

We first compute  $\mathbb{E}(S_A)$ . Let  $B=\{1, 2, \cdots, n\} \backslash A$  (that is, the set containing all integers from  $1$  to  $n$  not in  $A$ ). Note that
\begin{align*} \sum_{A \subseteq \{1, 2, \cdots, n\}} S_A= \sum_{A \subseteq \{ 1, 2, \cdots, n\}} \left(\sum_{i \in A} x_i\right)^2 = 2^{n-1} \sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 + 2^{n-2} \sum_{\substack{i, j \in A  i \neq j}} 2x_ix_j = 2^{n-1} - 2^{n-2} = 2^{n-2}\end{align*}

\[a+b<a+c<b+c<b+d<c+d\]
yield at least  $3$  values of  $S_A^2$ . As it is clear that not all  $x_i$  are the same, we get either  $2$  or  $3$  distinct values of  $x_i$ . For a particular nonzero  $x_i$ , taking  $x_i,2x_i$  gives a contradiction to  $S_A^2 \in \{0,\lambda\}$ . We then throw away all zero  $x_i$ ; we can add them back later. We now get the following cases.**Case 1**: We have two nonzero  $x_i$ . Let those  $x_i$  be  $a<b$ . We get  $a+b=0,a^2+b^2=1$ . Thus,  $a=-1/\sqrt{2},b=1/\sqrt{2}$ . The possible values of  $S_A^2$  are  $0,1/2$ , thus we get equality for
\[\{x_1,\dots , x_n\} = \left\{-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},0,\cdots , 0\right\}\]
and  $\lambda = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$  with some number of  $0$ s. Indeed, we have  $2^{n-2} = 2^{n-3}/\lambda^2$  possible sets  $A$ ;  $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$  and some choice of  $0$ s from the  $n-2$  instances of  $0$ .**Case 2**: We have three nonzero  $x_i$ . Let those  $x_i$  be  $a<b<c$ . As  $a+b<a+c<b+c$ , we get  $a+c=0$  and  $a+b=-(b+c)$  by the information about  $S_A^2$ . This yields  $0=(a+b)+(b+c) = (a+b+c)+b = b$ , absurd.


Hence, we have the one equality case described earlier.

**Claim: ** $\sum _{A\subseteq\{1, 2, \ldots, n\}} S_A^2= 2^{n-2}.$ *Proof:*Remark that $$ \mathbb{E}[S_A^2] = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{1 \leq i \leq n} x_i^2 + \frac{1}{2} \sum_{1 \leq i \neq j \leq n} x_ix_j = \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{4} = \frac{1}{4}. $$ Thus by linearity of expectation on the $2^n$ subsets, we have proven our desired claim. Now remark that $S_A$ and $S_{\{1, 2, \ldots, n\} \setminus A}$ have opposite signs, exactly one must be positive (of course, unless both are $0$ ). Now, we are home free: let $k$ be the number of subsets $A$ such that $S_A \geq 0$ and $S_A^2 \geq \lambda^2$ ; now $k \leq \frac{2^{n-3}}{\lambda^2}$ , as desired. Denote  $\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} = a.$  The equality cases are:


- $\{x_{1}, x_{2}\} = \{a, -a\},$  and  $\lambda = a.$  We have  $\frac{2^{n-3}}{\lambda^{2}} =1,$  and there is  $1$  set with  $S_{A} \ge \lambda.$

Next, we will prove the that there are at most  $\frac{2^{n-3}}{\lambda^{2}}$  sets  $A$  which satisfy the condition. **Claim:**The sums of  $(S_{A}-\lambda)$  and  $(S_{A}-\lambda)^{2}$  over all sets  $S$  are  $-2^{n}\lambda$  and  $2^{n-2}+2^{n}\lambda^{2}.$ **Proof:**The expected value of  $(S_{A}-\lambda)$  is  $-\lambda,$  so the sum of  $(S_{A}-\lambda)$  is  $-2^{n}\lambda.$  As for the other sum:
    \begin{align*}
        \sum_{A \subseteq [n]}(S_{A}-\lambda)^{2} &= \sum_{A\subseteq[n]}(S_{A}^{2}-2S_{A}\lambda + \lambda^{2}) & = \sum_{A \subseteq [n]}S_{A}^{2}-2\lambda \sum_{A \subseteq[n]}S_{A}+2^{n}\lambda^{2}&=\sum_{A\subseteq [n]} \sum_{i \in A}x_{i}^{2} + \sum_{i,j \in A} 2x_{i}x_{j} +2^{n}\lambda^{2}&=2^{n-1}\sum_{i\in A}x_{i}^{2} + 2^{n-2} \sum_{i,j \in A} 2x_{i}x_{j} + 2^{n}\lambda^{2}& = 2^{n-1} \cdot 1 + 2^{n-2} \cdot (-1) + 2^{n} \lambda^{2} & = 2^{n-2}+2^{n}\lambda^{2}.
    \end{align*} $\square$ Now, let  $d_{A} = S_{A} - \lambda.$  Then,  $d_{A} + d_{[n]/A} = -2\lambda.$  So, let  $\{a_{1},\dots,a_{2^{n-1}}\}$  and  $\{-2\lambda-a_{1}, \dots, -2\lambda-a_{2^{n-1}}\}$  together form the set of  $d_{A},$  assuming that  $a_{i} \ge -2\lambda-a_{i},$  implying that  $a_{i} \ge -\lambda.$  Now, we have that  $a_{1}^{2} + \dots +a_{n}^{2}+(-2\lambda-a_{1})^{2}+\dots+(-2\lambda-a_{n})^{2} = 2a_{1}^{2}+\cdots+2a_{n}^{2}+4\lambda(a_{1}+\dots+a_{n}) + 4\lambda^{2} \cdot 2^{n-1} = 2^{n}\lambda^{2}+2^{n-2},$ or   $$ \sum_{i=1}^{2^{n-1}} (a_{i}+\lambda)^{2} = 2^{n-3}. $$   Now, if  $a_{i}$  is nonnegative, then  $(a_{i}+\lambda)^{2} \ge \lambda^{2}.$  So, we can have at most  $\frac{2^{n-3}}{\lambda^{2}}$  nonnegative  $a_{i}.$

stem_md:
Several children were playing in the ugly tree when suddenly they all fell.
  $\bullet$  Roger hit branches  $A$ ,  $B$ , and  $C$  in that order on the way down.
  $\bullet$  Sue hit branches  $D$ ,  $E$ , and  $F$  in that order on the way down.
  $\bullet$  Gillian hit branches  $G$ ,  $A$ , and  $C$  in that order on the way down.
  $\bullet$  Marcellus hit branches  $B$ ,  $D$ , and  $H$  in that order on the way down.
  $\bullet$  Juan-Phillipe hit branches  $I$ ,  $C$ , and  $E$  in that order on the way down.
Poor Mikey hit every branch A through  $I$  on the way down. Given only this information, in how many different orders could he have hit these 9 branches on the way down?
solution_md:
Solution 1:

In order from tallest off the ground, we obtain the following inequalities: $A>B>C$ ,  $D>E>F$ ,  $G>A>C$ ,  $B>D>H$ ,  $I>C>E$ From this, we obtain the following inequality chain: $G>A>B>C>E>F$ We now have to insert  $D, H, I$  somewhere in the inequality chain, such that the following conditions apply:

(1) $B>D>E,F,H$ (2) $I>C>E$ Note that the conditions  $D>F$  and  $I>E$  follow from  $D>E$  and  $I>C$  respectively, so our new condition list is:

(1) $B>D>E, H$ (2) $I>C$ I use some casework here.    $D$  seems to be the easiest to do casework on, since there are two spots we can have  $D$ .

Case 1:   $G>A>B>D>C>E>F$ Now, we have  $D>H$  and  $I>C$ .  For the case that  $D>I>C$ , then we can have  $D>H>I>C$ ,  $D>I>H>C$ , or we can have  $D>I>C>H>E>F$ ,  $D>I>C>E>H>F$ ,  $D>I>C>E>F>H$  for a total of  $5$  ways.  

When we don't have  $D>I>C$ , we have  $I>C$  so there is  $4$  spots for  $I$  (it can be directly before  $D$ , directly before  $B$ , directly before  $A$ , or directly before  $G$ ).  We also have   $4$  spots for  $H$  (directly before  $C$ , directly before  $E$ , directly before  $F$  after  $F$ ) for a total of  $4*4=16$  and gives a case total of  $21$ .  

Case 2:   $G>A>B>C>D>E>F$ Since  $D>H$ , we have  $3$  spots for  $H$  (after  $D$  after  $E$  after  $F$ ) and  $4$  spots for  $I$  (before  $C$ , before  $B$ , before  $A$ , before  $G$ ), for a total of  $12$  for this case.

Summing up the two cases gives  $\boxed{33}$ .

Solution 2:  

We get the inequalities: $A>B>C$ ,  $D>E>F$ ,  $G>A>C$ ,  $B>D>H$ ,  $I>C>E$ Using this, we deduce the inequality:   $G>A>B>D>H$ .  We separate this into  $3$  cases on  $C$ .

Case 1:   $G>A>B>C>D>H$ .

This gives since  $D>E>F$ , we get that we can have  $D>E>F>H$ ,  $D>E>H>F$ ,  $D>H>E>F$  for  $3$  choices there.  For  $I$  now, we have  $4$  choices, we can have  $G>A>B>I>C$ ,  $G>A>I>B>C$ ,  $G>I>A>B>C$ ,  $I>G>A>B>C$ .  Therefore, there is a total of  $3*4=12$  for this case.  

Case 2:   $G>A>B>D>C>H$ Now,  $I$  has  $5$  choices instead, it can be directly after  $D$ , directly after  $B$ , directly after  $A$ , directly after  $G$ , or before  $G$ .  Also, since  $C>E$ , again we get three choices for  $EF$  therefore we get a total of  $3*5=15$  in this case.  

Case 3:   $G>A>B>D>H>C$ Since  $C>E>F$ , we must have  $G>A>B>D>H>C>E>F$ .  We also have  $I>C$ , therefore we have  $6$  choices now for where  $I$  is (directly after  $H$ , directly after  $D$ , directly after  $B$ , directly after  $A$ , directly after  $G$ , directly before  $G$ ).  Therefore we get  $6*1=6$  for this case.  

Summing these up, we get  $\boxed{33}$  as before.

stem_md: In quadrilateral  $ABCD$ ,  $\angle DAB=\angle ABC=110^{\circ}$ ,  $\angle BCD=35^{\circ}$ ,  $\angle CDA=105^{\circ}$ , and  $AC$  bisects  $\angle DAB$ . Find  $\angle ABD$ .
solution_md: Notice $$ \angle BCA = 180^{\circ} - \angle CAB - \angle ABC = 180^{\circ} - \frac{110^{\circ}}{2} - 110^{\circ} = 15^{\circ}. $$ Now, let $E$ lie on $AD$ such that $AB = AE$ . It's easy to see $ABCE$ is a kite, so $\angle ACE = \angle BCA = 15^{\circ}$ .**Claim:** $BCDE$ is cyclic. *Proof.* Notice $$ \angle AEB = \angle ABE = \frac{180^{\circ} - 110^{\circ}}{2} = 35^{\circ} = \angle BCD $$ and the result easily follows. $\square$ Thus, $$ \angle EBD = \angle ECD = \angle ACD - \angle ACE = (\angle BCD - \angle BCA) - 15^{\circ} = (35^{\circ} - 15^{\circ}) - 15^{\circ} = 5^{\circ}. $$ Thus, $\angle ABD = \angle ABE + \angle EBD = 35^{\circ} + 5^{\circ} = \boxed{40^{\circ}.}$ $\blacksquare$ **Remarks:** I found this solution by playing around with various "nice" constructions and some trial/error. Eventually, I observed that $$ 110^{\circ} + 2 \cdot 35^{\circ} = 180^{\circ} $$ holds, motivating the construction of $E$ .

candidates: <details><summary>My Solution</summary>Construct  $CD'$  parallel to  $AB$  with  $D'$  on line  $AD$ . After drawing in some lines and some trivial angle chasing we find that triangle  $ACD'$  has  $AD'=CD'$ . Since trapezoid  $ABCD'$  is isosceles we also have  $AD'=BC$  so by transitivity  $BC=CD'$ . I claim that triangles  $BCD$  and  $D'CD$  are congruent. Indeed, angle chasing tells us that  $\angle{DCD'}=\angle{BCD}$ , we have from above that  $BC=CD'$ , and they share the segment  $CD$ . By SAS they are congruent, so  $\angle{CD'D}=\angle{CBD}$ . Since it is easy to find  $\angle{CD'D}=70$  with angle chasing, we conclude that  $\angle{ABD}=110-\angle{CBD}=110-70=\boxed{40}$</details>

<details><summary>My solution</summary>First notice that because  $AC$  bisects  $\angle DAB$ , we have  $\angle BAC=\angle DAC=110^\circ/2=55^\circ$ , and consequently,
\[
\angle ACB=180^\circ-\angle BAC-\angle ABC=180^\circ-55^\circ-110^\circ=15^\circ
\]
and
\[
\angle DCA=180^\circ-\angle DAC-\angle ADC=180^\circ-55^\circ-105^\circ = 20^\circ.
\]

Note that quadrilateral  $ABCD$  is split into two triangles  $ABC$  and  $ADC$ . Let  $D'$  be the reflection of  $B$  over line  $AC$ , so that triangles  $ABC$  and  $AD'C$  are congruent. Because triangle  $ABD'$  is iscoseles, it follows that 
\[
\angle ABD' = \frac{1}{2}(180^\circ-\angle BAD')=\frac{1}{2}(180^\circ-110^\circ)=35^\circ.
\]
Furthermore, 
\[
\angle DCD' = \angle DCA-\angle ACD'=\angle DCA -\angle ACB=20^\circ-15^\circ = 5^\circ.
\]
Now, since 
\[
\angle CBD'+\angle CDD'=\angle ABC-\angle ABD'+\angle CDD'=110^\circ-35^\circ+105^\circ=180^\circ,
\]
quadrilateral  $BCDD'$  is cyclic. When we draw the circle, we see that angles  $\angle DBD'$  and  $\angle DCD'$  are inscribed in the same arc; hence, they are equal. But we already found that  $\angle DCD'=5^\circ$ , so we also have  $\angle DBD'=5^\circ$ . Finally, we can compute
\[
\angle ABD=\angle ABD'+\angle DBD'=35^\circ+5^\circ=\boxed{40^\circ}.
\]</details>

Alternate Solution: By the Law of Sines, we have the following equations:

1)  $\frac{AD}{\sin 20^{\circ}} = \frac{CD}{\sin 55^{\circ}}$  $\newline
\newline$ 2)  $\frac{AB}{\sin 15^{\circ}} = \frac{BC}{\sin 55^{\circ}}$ Isolating  $\sin 55^{\circ}$  from equations 1 and 2 and setting these quantities equal yields:

3)  $\frac{\sin 20^{\circ} \cdot CD}{AD} = \frac{\sin 15^{\circ} \cdot BC}{AB} \implies \frac{AB}{AD} \cdot \sin 20^{\circ} = \frac{BC}{CD} \cdot \sin 15^{\circ}$ However, by another application of the Law of Sines on  $\triangle ACD$  and  $\triangle ABC$ , we have:

4)  $\frac{CD}{\sin 55^{\circ}} = \frac{AC}{\sin 105^{\circ}}$  $\newline
\newline$ 5)  $\frac{BC}{\sin 55^{\circ}} = \frac{AC}{\sin 105^{\circ}}$ Cross multiplication and equating equations 4 and 5 gives us the following: $BC \cdot \sin 110^{\circ} = CD \cdot \sin 105^{\circ} \implies \frac{BC}{CD} = \frac{\sin 105^{\circ}}{\sin 110^{\circ}}$ Plugging this into equation 3, we have: $\frac{AB}{AD} = \frac{\sin 15^{\circ} \cdot \sin 105^{\circ}}{\sin 20^{\circ} \cdot \sin 110^{\circ}}$ By product to sum identities and using utilizing some basic trig relationships:  $\cos \theta = - \cos (180^{\circ} - \theta)$  and  $\sin \theta = \cos (90^{\circ} - \theta)$ , we can simply the above expression greatly. $\frac{AB}{AD} = \frac{\sin 15^{\circ} \cdot \sin 105^{\circ}}{\sin 20^{\circ} \cdot \sin 110^{\circ}} 
\implies
\frac{AB}{AD} = \frac{\cos 120^{\circ}}{\cos 130^{\circ}}
\implies
\frac{AB}{AD} = \frac{\cos 60^{\circ}}{\cos 50^{\circ}}
\implies
\frac{AB}{AD} = \frac{\sin 30^{\circ}}{\sin 40^{\circ}}
\implies
\frac{AB}{\sin 30^{\circ}} = \frac{AD}{\sin 40^{\circ}}$ Finally, by the Law of Sines, this implies that  $\angle ABD = \boxed{40^{\circ}}$ .

As you can see, v_Enhance's solution is entirely motivated by thinking about cyclic quads. This is not the natural way that mathematics is done, and Euclid certainly did not think about cyclic quadrilaterals as tools for proving a theorem. This is the difference between the "dialectic" of competition maths and that of "real" maths. Basically, competition maths has a completely different set of "axioms" than higher maths. I do not mean this literally: competition maths is after all a subset of maths in general. But when it comes to solving problems, the generalities you start from in order to work your way towards the specific problem in question are completely different from the generalities an actual mathematician would use. A mathematician would not start by thinking about cyclic quadrilaterals, but would instead try to construct the figure, because construction is the natural way of proceeding from generalities to specific things within Euclidean geometry. If one wants to use the dialectic of competition maths and start from competition configurations such as cyclic quadrilaterals, rather than the fountain of geometry itself which is construction, then that is their choice. While this competition approach may give seemingly more elegant solutions due to its alignment with how the problem itself was likely written, this is not really elegance because it relies on artificiality. True elegance is when beauty stems from mathematics itself rather than some quirk which is due to how the problem was written.

Here is a 100% motivated solution which uses the natural way of construction in geometry.

We start by seeing that the bisector condition and the equal angles conditions are entirely artificial. Thus, we instead focus on how the desired angle is determined from the configuration (which is equivalent to seeing how it is constructed from it). This is obvious, because as soon as the quadrilateral is drawn, the desired angle is immediately determined as well. Thus, all we need to do is to compute it by assuming that the side lengths etc of the quadrilateral are given and working our way towards the desired angle.

Let DA=a, AB=b, BC=c, CD=d. Also let the desired angle be x. Let the angles be named according to their vertex, so  $\angle DAB=A$  etc. We easily find that the desired angle satisfies  $\tan x = \frac{\sin A}{\frac{b}{a}-\cos A}$ . Further, we find that  $\frac{b}{a}=\frac{\sin D\sin \angle ACB}{\sin \angle DCA\sin A}$ . Having completed the main part of the problem of "constructing" the desired angle from the givens of the diagram, we now simply need to compute this by using the artificial conditions mentioned earlier.

We get  $\tan x = \frac{\sin 110}{\frac{\sin 105\sin 15}{\sin 20\sin 110}-\cos 110}$ . We immediately notice that the  $\sin 105\sin 15$  is "ugly" and doesn't seem to fit in with the  $\sin 110$ 's. But what about the  $\sin 20$ ? We want to somehow relate this to  $110$ . Perhaps  $90+20=110$  would be useful? We find  $\sin 20=\sin(110-90)=-\sin (90-110)=-\cos 110$ . Letting  $\cos 110=c$  and  $\sin 110=s$  we have  $\tan x = \frac{s}{\frac{\sin 105\sin 15}{-cs}-c}$ .

Now we simply try to get  $\sin 105\sin 15$  in terms of  $s,c$ . Here we will again use the constructive approach by seeing how  $105$  and  $15$  stem from the givens of the problem. The givens are the angles of the quadrilateral, including  $55$  which is just  $\frac{110}{2}$ . So we have  $\sin 105\sin 15=\sin (55+20)\sin (110+55)$ , and expanding this we get  $\frac{s}{2}(s^2-c^2)-c^2s$ . Finally, plugging this into our expression for  $\tan x$  gives  $\frac{2cs}{c^2-s^2}=\frac{\sin 220}{\cos 220}=\tan 220=\tan (220-180)=\tan 40$  and we are done.  $\square$ As you can see, we did end up using problem solving heuristics to solve the problem, namely by noticing the ugly expression within the expression for  $\tan x$ . Unfortunately, this is as general as it gets, and while we avoided having to use the dialectic of "competition Euclidean geometry" (cyclic quads and all), we cannot escape from the dialectic of "problem solving" completely, because after all, the desired angle is only determined because of the given artificial information. However, as you can see, we managed to reduce the artificial nature of thinking in terms of cyclic quads to an entirely general problem solving heuristic of simply noticing that something was ugly and trying to make it fit in with the rest of the expression, and this immediately led to the goal.

By the way, for those who want further clarification of what I mean by "generalities" of a subject, think about how primes are used in number theory problems. The exact same thing applies to geometry, except here the generalities are points, lines etc, and so construction is the most natural way of proceeding from generalities to particularities within geometry. In number theory, it is prime factorization instead.
The cyclic quad construction in post 4 is equivalent to noticing and using the fact that  $C$  is the  $A$ -excenter of  $\triangle DAB$ .

Here is another motivated construction, this time starting from the artificial conditions.

We want to construct the desired angle. We start by drawing an angle A of 110 degrees and bisecting it with an arbitrary line.

Next we cut off a length 1 from the right side of angle A to get point B and make angle B 110 degrees. This determines a point C which is the intersection of angle B and the bisector of angle A. Thus, we immediately have the lengths BC and AC, which are easily found using the sine rule as  $BC=\frac{\sin 55}{\sin 15}$  and  $AC=\frac{\sin 110}{\sin 15}$ .

Now the final step for constructing our angle is to draw an angle of 20 degrees at point C so that angle C as a whole is 35 degrees. This immediately determines the whole quadrilateral by the intersection of this new angle with the left side of angle A. Let this intersection point be D. We have now fully determined the desired angle  $\theta$  as well as lengths  $AD, CD, BD$ . We simply need to calculate the desired angle using the 20 degree angle, which is what determined it.

So using the sine rule on ABD, ADC and BCD respectively gives:

1.  $\frac{\sin \theta}{AD}=\frac{\sin 110}{BD}$ 2.  $\frac{AD}{\sin 20}=\frac{\sin 110}{\sin 15\sin 105}$ 3.  $\frac{\sin 55}{\sin 15\sin (35+\theta)}=\frac{BD}{\sin 35}$ and multiplying them all together gives $\frac{\sin \theta\sin 55}{\sin 20\sin 15\sin (35+\theta)}=\frac{\sin 110\sin 110}{\sin 15\sin 105\sin 35}$  $\frac{\sin \theta\sin 55\cos 55}{\sin (35+\theta)}=\frac{\sin 110\sin 20\cos 20}{\sin 105}$  $\frac{\sin \theta}{\sin (35+\theta)}=\frac{\sin 40}{\sin 105}$  $\sin \theta\sin 105=\sin 40(\sin 35\cos \theta+\sin \theta\cos 35)$  $\tan \theta\sin 75=\sin 40\sin 35+\sin 40\tan \theta\cos 35$  $\tan \theta \sin (35+40)=\sin 40\sin 35+\sin 40\tan \theta \cos 35$  $\tan \theta\sin 35\cos 40=\sin 40\sin 35$  $\tan \theta = \tan 40$ .

The constructive approach can also be used to motivate this Euclidean geometry solution. I will post the motivation later.

Draw a cyclic trapezium  $ABCD$  determined by CDA=70, ABC=110 and BCA-15 (note we need to specify BCA otherwise the trapezium is not determined fully: it could be either very flat or very long). Now choose point  $P$  on side  $BC$  so that triangle  $PAC$  is isosceles with PAC=PCA=15. Draw a circle centre  $P$  and radius PA=PC and let it intersect side AD of the trapezium at Q. This is the construction part complete.

Now clearly, if ACQ=x then since angles at the centre are double we have APQ=2x. Then straight forward angle chasing using the isosceles triangles generated by the radii of the circle yields that AQP=70, in other words, ABPQ is also a cyclic trapezium. So immediately we have BPQ=70 giving x=20, and also, ABQ=APQ=2x=40.
Note: In post #16, "first attached diagram" refers to the one without the four stages of construction.

One realizes that post #16 is basically an investigation of how the problem stems from a point, rather than a line etc. Only by determining the whole configuration from a point can we truly be said to have constructed the problem. So the four stages in post #16 are a true construction, whereas all the others (post #15, 14 and 11) are not really true constructions, but only "makeshift" ones which start more or less from the configuration as given.

<details><summary>Solution</summary>Denote  $\angle ADB = x$  and chase all angles. WLOG take  $AB=1$ . From LoS in  $\triangle ABC$ , we get  $\frac{1}{\sin 15}=\frac{AC}{\sin 110}$ . From LoS in  $\triangle ACD$ , we get  $\frac{AD}{\sin 20}=\frac{AC}{\sin 105}=\frac{AC}{\sin 75}$ . Combining these two gives  $AD=4 \sin 110 \sin 20$ , and from LoS in  $\triangle ABD$  we get  $\frac{1}{\sin x}=\frac{AD}{\sin{(70-x)}}$ . This is equivalent to  $\frac{\sin{(70-x)}}{\sin x}=4 \sin 110 \sin 20$ , or  $\frac{\sin{(70-x)}}{\sin x}=-2 \cos 130$ . This is equal to  $\sin{(70-x)}=2 \sin x \cos 50$ , or  $\sin(70-x)=\sin(x+50)+\sin(x-50)$ . This is the same as  $\sin(70-x)-\sin(x+50)=\sin(x-50)$ , or  $2 \sin(10-x) \cos 60 = \sin(x-50)$  from Difference-to-Product. We have  $\sin 60 = \frac{1}{2}$ , so  $\sin(10-x)=\sin(x-50)$ , and hence  $10-x = x-50 \implies x=30$ . We have  $\angle ABD = 70-x=\boxed{40}$ , and we're done.</details>

We take  $E$  on  $AC$  so that  $ABED$  is a cyclic quadrilateral implying  $\angle BED=70$ . As  $ABED$  is a cyclic quadrilateral,  $\angle DBE=\angle BDE=55$  which means  $\triangle BED$  is an isosceles triangle. So we can transplant  $E$  as a center of a circle and  $C$  as a random point in the circumference of that circle (im not sure if this is trivial or not tho : [ , thus the **lemma** below ) so  $\angle AED=40=\angle ABD$ **Lemma**: Let  $BED$  be an isosceles triangle and  $C$  be a point on the side of  $BD$  where  $E$  lies and such that  $\angle BED=2\angle BCD$  then there is a circle where  $E$  is the center and  $C$  as a point on its circumference.**Proof**: We show that if  $BED$  be an isosceles triangle and  $\angle BED=2\angle BCD$  then  $C$  must lie on the circle's circumference.
Suppose  $C$  doesnt lie on the circumference, then draw a line through  $C$  and let it intersect the circumference at point  $F$  and  $G$ . We know  $2\angle BFD=\angle BED$ . We can clearly see  $\angle BFG > \angle BCF$  (if  $C$  is outside the circle) and  $\angle DFG> \angle DCF$  so  $\angle BFD> \angle BCD$  (if  $C$  was inside the circle then following the same process we would have derived at  $\angle BFD<\angle BCD$ ) implying what we wanted to show.

The perpendicular from  $A$  to  $AC$  touches  $CD$ ,  $CB$  at  $E$ ,  $F$ , then  $\Delta DAB$  is the orthic triangle because  $\angle DAB=180^{\circ}-2\cdot\angle DCB$ , so  $\angle DBA= 180^{\circ}-2\angle DEA=\boxed{40^{\circ}}$ .    $_{\blacksquare}$

solution_md: <details><summary>Solution</summary>Find the side length of the big triangle. Since each axle is halfway through the smaller triangles, the side length of the big triangle is  $30+9+9=48$ . Now, find the circumference of the circumscribed circle, which is the path the dot will follow to reach it's original position. To do this we must find the diameter of the circumscribed circle, which is  $\frac{3}{2}$  of the length from the dot to the bottom of the big triangle (call this length  $x$ ).  $x$  can be found by using the Pythagorean Theorem, with  $\left( \frac{48}{2} \right)^2+x^2=48^2$ . Simplifying this gives us  $x^2=\frac{3}{4}(48^2)$ , which further simplifies to  $x^2=\frac{3}{4}(48)(48)=3(12)(48)=2(2)(2)(2)(2)(2)(3)(3)(3)=2^6(3^3)$ . This now reveals that  $x=2^3(3)\sqrt{3}=24\sqrt{3}$ . Now, plugging this in gives us  $D=\frac{3}{2}(24\sqrt{3})=36\sqrt{3}$ , where  $D$  is the diameter of the circumscribed circle. Now, all that's left is to find the circumference, which is  $36\sqrt{3}(\pi)$ , giving us our answer of  $\boxed{36\pi\sqrt{3}}$ .</details>

solution_md:
<u>Lemma:</u> A quadruple  $(y_1, y_2, y_3, y_4)$  is quadratic iff  $y_1-3y_2+3y_3-y_4=0$ .

<u>Proof:</u> Clearly $(a+b+c)-3(4a+2b+c)+3(9a+3b+c)-(16a+4b+c)=$   $a(1-12+27-16)+b(1-6+9-4)+c(1-3+3-1)=0$ .

In the other direction, there's exactly one quadratic function  $q(x)$  with  $q(1)=y_1$ ,  $q(2)=y_2$ ,  $q(3)=y_3$ .  It is  $y_1+(y_2-y_1)(x-1)+\frac{y_3-2y_2+y_1}{2}(x-1)(x-2)$ .  This is because the difference between any two quadratics fulfilling these equations has three roots, so is the null polynomial; also, clearly, this polynomial satisfies it.  Then plugging in  $q(4)$  gives  $y_1+(y_2-y_1)(4-1)+\frac{y_3-2y_2+y_1}{2}(4-1)(4-2)$   $=y_1+3(y_2-y_1)+3(y_3-2y_2+y_1)=3y_3-3y_2+y_1$ .

So we'd need  $y_4=3y_3-3y_2+y_1$ , as stated.

<u>End Lemma</u>

So clearly if  $a_{ij}$  is the entry in the  $i$ th row in the  $j$ th column, then we must prove that  $a_{14}-3a_{24}+3a_{34}-a_{44}=0$ .  But

\begin{align*}a_{14}-3a_{24}+3a_{34}-a_{44}&=a_{14}-3a_{24}+3a_{34}-a_{44}
&-3(a_{13}-3a_{23}+3a_{33}-a_{43})
&+3(a_{12}-3a_{22}+3a_{32}-a_{42})
&-(a_{11}-3a_{21}+3a_{31}-a_{41})
&
&=a_{14}-3a_{13}+3a_{12}-a_{11}
&-3(a_{24}-3a_{23}+3a_{22}-a_{21})
&+3(a_{34}-3a_{33}+3a_{32}-a_{31})
&-(a_{44}-3a_{43}+3a_{42}-a_{41})
&=0\end{align*}

so we're done.

solution_md:
<details><summary>Simon Says</summary>Assume that  $a\ge3$ . Then  $\left(1+\frac{1}{a}\right)\left(1+\frac{1}{b}\right)\left(1+\frac{1}{c}\right)\le \left(1+\frac{1}{a}\right)^3\le\left(\frac{4}{3}\right)^3=\frac{64}{27}<3$ , a contradiction.

We now have two cases.
